items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — Some 36 years in and still going strong. The now legendary SIGH has become nearly synonymous withJapanese avant-garde metal with a knack for melding the most unlikely of sounds together in acohesive whole and still finding new ways to take the fanbase somewhere the band has not yetexplored. Once again the crazed black metal turned experimental sonic wizards led by the inimitableMirai Kawashima returns with its 14th release GOH-KA, another hi-brow conceptual masterwork thattranslates as something akin to "infernal fire scorching the sinners" or simply "karma." The albumdelves into the darker concepts of Buddhism including the concepts adapted from the Buddhist hellscrolls and through a series of 11 tracks this team of five presents a fiery hellish journey thatforges a fiery path through the crossroads of bands such as Celtic Frost, Voivod, second wave blackmetal and traditional Japanese music.It's the usual maelstrom of anything goes in the SIGH universe although GOH-KA retains the morefocused approach of tightly woven concept albums of recent years. You can expect the usualthunderous roar of black metal guitar works along with a pounding bass and drum accompaniment butSIGH delves deep into its Japanese heritage with ample traditional instruments woven into the mixalong with moments that eschew the metal paradigm completely with large chunks of "Anzenshokon" forexample sounding more like a movie soundtrack before trading off with the first wave black metalapproach that has been its bailiwick since its inception. Joining the SIGH team is bassist Fr�d�ricLeclercq (Kreator, Dragonforce), ex-Fear Factory drummer Mike Heller and Opeth mastermind Mikael�kerfeldt who delivers a ripping guitar solo on "Unputenpu" the album's lead single.SIGH traverses these brackish waters well and with the opening "Kuso-shi (1-3)" runs the gamut ofcrafty psychedelic rock laced avant-metal with epic classic Japanese traditionals interwoven into araspy narrative that together generate interesting melodic developments, stylish fusionfunctionality and epic transitions between varying stylistic approaches. Perhaps a mellower lessmetal dependent release from previous works but an effective expansion of the sonic palette whereatmospheric embellishments are allowed to shine like diamonds in the rough. The one constant that isthe thread between all SIGH albums are the raspy vocals of Kawashima's feisty spirited lyricaldelivers however there are many more backing vocal additions which give this album a much largerthan life production value. As always many metal purists may not deem GOH-KA as metal enough butlike many of SIGH's constructs, the metal is merely one vital ingredient to a much larger sonicedifice. Somewhat reminiscent of the band's best known release "Imaginary Soundscape," GOH-KA delivers asimilar kaleidoscopic approach where psychedelia, metal, traditional folk and progressive symphonicrock play together like Bambi and Godzilla in a universe of the band's own making and once againsomehow despite all the odds stacked against the whole shebang comes off as yet another triumphantvictory for this Tokyo based band that continues to punctuate the 21st century with some of the mostcutting edge sounds under the greater banner of metal music. Personally i find the expanded use oftraditional Japanese instruments and homegrown flavors to be the wise choice for this creative bandto delve into. Metal and folk music has been immensely popular for over three decades now but yetthe Japanese have been more reticent to traverse these developments however SIGH proves it has thechops to pull it all off with ease. Another excellent release from Tokyo's wildest metal band.

items._cn_summary: 日本先锋金属乐队SIGH的第十四张专辑《GOH-KA》以佛教地狱概念为线索，通过11首曲目构建混合黑金属、迷幻摇滚、前卫摇滚与传统日本音乐的声响旅程。开篇《Kuso-shi (1-3)》展现了从迷幻前卫金属到史诗式传统旋律的过渡，金属段落与电影原声感氛围并行，大量传统乐器与人声合唱增强戏剧性。与Kreator/Dragonforce贝斯手、Fear Factory鼓手及Opeth主唱合作，带来更宽广的演奏层次。相较早期作品，金属占比降低，氛围化与交响化编排更加突出，延续了《Imaginary Soundscape》的万花筒式路径。

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”

items._cn_summary: 这张回顾专辑收录了韩国作曲家兼演奏家金珍姬（Jin Hi Kim）四十年的创作与即兴作品，横跨五张作曲专辑与四张即兴录音。她将韩国传统乐器伽倻琴（文中为komungo，实为玄琴）引入电子音乐与实验即兴语境，通过计算机接口和信号处理扩展其音响边界。作品既保留韩国音乐的冥想气质，又与Kronos Quartet、Derek Bailey、Bill Frisell等当代音乐家展开深度对话，展现传统乐器与前卫语汇的碰撞。乐评强调她早年赴美学习电子音乐和作曲的经历，以及回顾过程中对自我创作脉络的重新发现，尤其欣赏其以有限的乐器音色与顶级即兴者交流的勇气。整体呈现一种基于内省能量与慢速虚无感的音乐叙事，是跨文化实验音乐的重要档案。

items.body:
This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Emilio Gordoa与已故Sven-Åke Johansson的二重奏录音，以“第三层”为概念，描述两位乐手在平行即兴线条之外浮现出的幽灵般第三维度。音乐近似于Erik Satie的家具音乐，通过重复材料与紧密共振营造出催眠般的、接近狂喜的聆听体验。乐评强调听众在集体即兴中的协作角色，认为这种音乐难以被言语完全界定，意义在流动与不可言说之间不断转化。作品创造了一种不寻常的声响空间，既透明又神秘，值得关注的是它在即兴互动中对深度聆听和共时书写式感知的独特探索。

items.body:
Gerry Hemingway leads a band of globe-trotters: German multi-reedist Frank Gratkowski whose recorded in the US often; pianist Izumi Kimura based in Ireland; Swiss bassist Christian Weber who’s recorded on three continents, crossing paths along the way with Yanks Oliver Lake, Ellery Eskelin, Nate Wooley, and Russ Johnson; Gerry himself, based in Lucerne since 2009.

In many ways Hemingway’s contemporary music mines his time in Anthony Braxton’s wondrous 1985-1993 quartet. The leaping staccato melody with asymmetrical phrases near the top of the 36-minute “Bau 4 Assembly” is one marker; another, the way that loose suite and the 23-minute “Slivers” use long improvised sections to tie together occasional scored episodes – not that Braxton was alone in that. And Braxton’s quartet prompted Hemingway’s duo with bandmate Marilyn Crispell, prefiguring his duo with Kimura in recent years.

On the CD, a six-minute Hemingway-Kimura improvisation is sandwiched between the long pieces, but I tend to cue up that “Third Story Variation” first, for its unbeatable interplay. The pianist and drummer catch and ride the same pulse, leaving plenty of air but also knowing how to fill various spaces along the way. Their timbral senses are fully compatible: her under-the-hood preparations tilt her sound drumward. They’ll set up a slow groove together, then she’ll use her other hand to play against it. It’s all very attentive and effective.

The longer pieces credited to Hemingway unfold like narratives, with discreet episodes, varied pacing, subgroup subplots, ways to build and dispel tension. “Slivers” is for trio, minus piano, Gratkowski leading off on squawky bass clarinet, tracked by Weber’s bass; the time feel is notably looser than the duo’s. A few minutes in, bass clarinet exits, and Frank’s re-entrance on disembodied wispy alto is placed just right: an instant orchestrator’s decision. Later there’s a section for low bass clarinet and arco bass in frictive unison under free drum rustle – suggesting Braxton’s love of the sub-basement, and the flexible trio dynamic of Gerry’s early/longtime vehicle BassDrumBone. But “Slivers” does slack off a bit between the scored tentpoles. There are times you wish the drummer would apply a firmer hand in a what-would-Billy-Higgins-do kind of way. One of Gerry’s signatures at the traps is a free-swinging–arms sense of relaxation, hitting the skins as if on the rebound, with some hits maybe dropped or delayed in transit. In the closing minutes, and on the closing theme, he can come off like someone who thinks he’s swinging harder than he is.

All four assemble for “Bau 4 Assembly” which makes up the bulk of the program. The venue Bau 4 in Altbüron, Switzerland was founded by folks in the timber business, and is located in their commercial compound. In tribute, Gerry and company play or use as beaters wood scraps retrieved from the workshop, notably heard around 10 minutes in, on a fast irregular clacky and texturally light colloquy which develops into something like pointillism with a groove (no small achievement) before flute and pedal-down piano soften things up. But not for long; in very short order, a scrapwood and piano gamelan. Midway, there’s a long-tone chapter with clarinet, and Gerry singing wavery lines into his cymbals or (says here) through metal objects, an odd effect he just about pulls off. (There’s a little Robert Wyatt in his vocal wah-wahs.) The composer and the quartet cover much ground. Elsewhere, a slow line’s melodic contours are subtly mirrored by the drums.

We won’t catalog every change-up or chapter, but near the end there’s a free-jazz blowout whose presence feels like checking a box – which is not to overlook Frank’s rapid multiphonic growls. (He’s got a great command of altissimo and pressurized reed textures.) Then they break into a loose brisk tempo, to frame that free-jazz energy. It arrives just where a non-drummer’s band would place a climactic the drum solo. Then a feint toward the Braxtonian head from half an hour earlier. A few staccato hits end things without a big fuss.

items.body: Vertical London does exactly what it says on the can, establishing its premise from the very first minutes through a recording of birds and planes over Loughborough Junction. It is a sound I immediately recognised after spending twenty years living beneath the same flight path in South London, but Kate Carr approaches this familiar collision without lamenting noise pollution or searching nostalgically for a disappearing city. Birds and aircraft occupy the same acoustic plane, each accepted as part of London’s everyday ecology. From there, Carr moves through Tube stations buried beneath the city, the Greenwich Foot Tunnel, shopping centres, parks and lifts inside the Shard, eventually looking back down at London stretching and twinkling below. Verticality becomes a way of listening to the city across its different levels. Although the record follows a journey across the capital, it never feels like a collection of sonic postcards. London identifies itself only in passing, through station announcements, tannoys mentioning the River Thames or fragments of public transport. People are everywhere, yet they seldom become protagonists. Conversations remain indistinct, with voices often arriving through loudspeakers instead of direct encounters. Titles such as “I don’t think you can hear but people largely discussed dogs all the way back to central London” quietly acknowledge the limitations of field recording itself: microphones never quite capture the same experience as the person carrying them. One of the album’s greatest pleasures lies in its humour. Carr’s wonderfully verbose titles continually reshape the act of listening. “Celebrating a squeaky transport barrier…”, “A very long queue for the London Eye which is quite shit…”, or “It was New Year’s Day after all, and yes someone really was playing this at the overground station” all display a dry self-deprecation that gently punctures any temptation towards field-recording solemnity. The joke is never directed at the sounds themselves, but at the expectations we bring to them. The album takes listening seriously without ever taking itself too seriously. A loose temporal framework also runs through the work. New Year’s Day appears only through fleeting details: someone wishing “Happy New Year” in Bloomsbury, an unexpected instrumental rendition of “Auld Lang Syne” at an Overground station. There are no celebrations or drunken crowds. The city simply carries on, making the choice of date feel quietly counterintuitive. Carr documents a public holiday through a London seemingly suspended between one year and the next. The only explicit intellectual companion appears during the visit to Kilburn. At one point Carr quietly records herself (assuming it is her voice) saying the neighbourhood’s name, almost as if she were leaving a spoken geotag for reference. It has the feel of an aide-mémoire accidentally left in the finished work, but it also introduces Doreen Massey into the album. From this point, ideas about place begin to inform the act of listening itself. Massey’s understanding of place as something continually produced through movement, memory and social relations quietly echoes throughout the record. Every location remains connected to the next. High-frequency tones drift between recordings, drones appear among the crows and dinosaurs of Crystal Palace, and even Hampstead is characterised by the whisper imposed by private security and the sense of controlled space. London emerges as a continuum, its locations connected through sound and movement. What I admire most about Vertical London is its trust in ordinary experience. Carr never appears to chase spectacular recordings. The only “climax” arrives midway through with a couple of “high drama” moments which are anything but. Both “Dramatic build-up to when I dipped into the shopping centre to find a man playing piano outside Aldi” and “Dramatic drummers on the street as I ran due to being late for my Shard viewing platform booking” animate the narrative with suitably understated theatricality. Carr allows the city to reveal itself through patient walking, public transport, chance encounters and small acts of attention. A squeaking ticket barrier, electromagnetic harmonics from the DLR and birds beneath aircraft all receive the same careful consideration. By the end of the journey, landmarks have receded into a living acoustic fabric, where every layer—from the tunnels beneath the streets to the flight paths overhead—contributes to the city’s constantly shifting identity. To walks us through the album, we have asked Kate Carr to answer a few questions for us by email. You are a dedicated walker. One of your recent sonic explorations has been Transect – Heathrow perimeter walk with bird horns. You have circled London and frequently go on walks when traveling whether that might be in Italy or China. For this album, which is not strictly speaking just a walk as public transport is an integral part of it, you’re constantly moving between birds and planes over Loughborough Junction, the deep Tube stations, the Greenwich Foot Tunnel beneath the Thames, lift shafts inside the Shard, and eventually looking out over the city from above. What made you decide verticality was going to become the organising idea this time round? Has living under the flight pathway in a city with an extensive underground system made you more conscious of what’s above and what’s below, so to speak? And did you have any expectations of the sounds, frequencies, resonances you were going to find? I think ever since I did my album Midsummer, London a few years back and went across the city from one side to another on that long summer solstice day, I was sort of mulling what other sorts of trajectories I could trace. I was thinking about this vertical one for a while as it is obviously on the face of it a very different journey to moving across the city, and I suppose I wondered just how different it would actually be, both the experience of undertaking it and also how different it might sound within the recordings themselves. Movement and journeys are really central to my work, I am always asking: what version of this route is my movement producing in a recording, this combination of the chance elements, how I am recording, what gear I am using, my own personhood and identity and what or who I encounter. For a long while now I am interested in recording as a trace of how all those things come together, and what aural fragments of these encounters and moments is recorded or indeed not recorded by the in the recording device. In terms of time spent at different verticalities, I have spent a lot of time obviously on the tube as most commuters have, but comparatively very little in London’s higher reaches. In doing the album I was interested in if elevation could be heard somehow or other, can something sound higher up? Or lower down? And I was also interested in the zigzag journey I was undertaking to bring me to these various elevations in the city. So it was a few different layers or questions to the project. I think yes you are probably very right that living under the the flight path has influenced my thinking about the vertical, I was actually planning at one point that the highest point in the album might be a recording from inside a plane, but once I decided to do it on New Year’s Day this was shelved as an idea. The final component to the album as I was thinking about it revolved around the darkness of winter in London, I liked the idea of getting higher and higher, and closer to the sun as a way of gesturing towards the difficulties of this long dark period, and then this idea of the new year, new me sort of thing, and how the experience of new year’s day itself sort of punctures this. In the jumble of all these things the project lurks. Human presence is felt, as it is to be expected since this is an urban work, but it is not always discernible, the only distinct speech one can hear come from “institutional” sources, loudspeakers, recorded voices, or formulaic propositions. Is this because of ethical concerns or purely for compositional purposes? There are some voices in it, just snippets of people passing me, one person wishing another happy new year, and the sorts of murmurs you hear when moving through locations. I did not deliberately leave out conversations in this work, but I do have ethical considerations in regard to this issue. My practice is centred on the traces of activities, encounters, moments which unfold in public space, both ones I can be heard in and ones I am not. I think there is something of value in recording in public space in this sort of fragmentary and incomplete way, but that said there are of course conversations and encounters which I would choose not to use and would not consider it ok for me to use. In this case it was a cold, dark and quiet day, I was moving fairly quickly through locations and what reached me were just these small fragments. The work is meant to convey the experience of commuting and I guess purposeful movement rather than the drift of psychogeography. Of course as we move through public space we do sometimes get drawn into listening to other people’s conversations, but here the work is more about an experience of being in my own head and thoughts, while also encountering these fragments of other people also going about their days. One thing that really struck me is just how funny Vertical London is. Not because anything overtly comic happens, but because your titles quietly reframe what we’re about to hear. “Celebrating a squeaky transport barrier”, “A very long queue for the London Eye which is quite shit…”, “Dramatic build-up to when I dipped into the shopping centre to find a man playing piano outside Aldi…”—they all have this wonderfully dry, self-deprecating humour that somehow makes you listen more carefully rather than less. Field recording and sound art can sometimes take themselves rather seriously, yet Vertical London never does. It seems to embrace chance, anticlimax and the absurdity of everyday urban life without diminishing the act of listening itself. Do the titles emerge naturally from the walks, or have they become your way of gently keeping both the practice of field recording—and yourself—in check? Ha, well I am glad you found it funny. I do find humour just a really important component of basically just life. Not in a distancing way, or even in a not taking things seriously way but more just than humour and delight are part of the fabric of existence. I basically very often am quite astonished by people and what they do and say, and how different we all are from the smallest to the biggest things, and taking a trip and how this unfolds is no different. I find what people do, how they are in public space, how we encounter each other and organise ourselves sometimes just really charming, of course other times quite sad or even surreal. I think undertaking this very random project on New Year’s Day just sort of adds to that feeling. Here I am racing to these different parts of London for no real reason except to see what they sound like and what is happening in them, encountering all sorts of people doing their own things, and in all of that there are just really absurd and bizarrely anticlimatic moments, as well moment of rushing and drama. I don’t really feel I need to keep myself in check, or that sound art is too serious or takes itself too seriously, I just think humour is part of my orientation towards the world and others. I title the works after finishing the piece, but they come easily to me really. They just emerge from my memories of the day, both the felt memories and the narrative ones. I really like and enjoy the relationship between words and the sound work itself. I have always enjoyed that aspect of making work. I am basically obsessed with words, so I love to feel the dynamic between the composition itself and the words which accompany it and what this relation generates in terms of an experience of the work. What made you decide to set this work within a 24-hour timeframe, choosing New Year’s day as its anchoring point especially when Vertical London doesn’t feel particularly jubilant or hangover? I was going to possibly do it on the winter solstice so it matched my summer solstice work, and that would have been good as well, but I missed this date as I was busy I think and so I decided on New Year’s Day as I felt this trajectory of moving upwards resonated in quite interesting ways with ideas of new year’s resolutions, new starts, renewal. I did like the dry humour or irony which emerged in undertaking the work where this movement upwards was revealed as a shift into increasingly sterile, managed and privatised spaces. Increasing altitude does not prove revelatory or even particularly uplifting in this work. In terms of the day long time frame, I tend to work with these strict limitations nowadays because I like how the paucity of time infuses the work. It makes it difficult to position the work as an attempt at some sort of ‘portrait’ of London in a definitive way. The strictness of the protocol for me lends the work these connotations of the fragmentary, the gesture, the moment, the random, the arbitrary. In my work I am always seeking to emphasise: here is my journey, full of moments, charm, annoyances, yes absurdities and surreal slices of existence but it is not London itself, just one version of London authored in time, movement and space. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._cn_summary: Kate Carr的《Vertical London》以垂直维度重新组织对伦敦的声音聆听，起点是 Loughborough Junction上空交织的鸟鸣与飞机轨迹——两种声音被并置于同一声学平面，既非控诉噪音污染，也不怀旧地追忆消逝中的城市。专辑随后穿越地下铁车站、格林威治人行隧道、购物中心、公园与碎片大厦电梯间，最终俯瞰伦敦全景。城市身份仅以车站广播、泰晤士河提示音与公共交通碎片隐约浮现，行人虽无处不在却不成为主角，模糊的对话多经由扬声器传来。幽默感贯穿作品，冗长而自嘲的标题持续改写聆听的姿态，轻巧地戳破田野录音易陷的庄严感。新年这一时间框架仅以零星细节勾勒——Bloomsbury的新年祝福、Overground车站意外响起的《Auld Lang Syne》器乐演奏——城市于节日中悬停于年份交替之间。录音者本人的声音在Kilburn短暂出现，宛若口语化的地理标记，留下备忘般的痕迹。

items.excerpt: Review by kenethlevine — While one can never accuse JOANNA NEWSOM of adopting conventional voice and arrangements on a path to surprisingly broad cult acceptance, "Divers", still her most recent, is refreshingly accessible in both arenas. items.body: Review by kenethlevine — While one can never accuse JOANNA NEWSOM of adopting conventional voice and arrangements on a path to surprisingly broad cult acceptance, "Divers", still her most recent, is refreshingly accessible in both arenas. While she has retained her core idiosyncrasies, since "Have one on Me" her retooled pipes, emphasis on more conventional song structures and reliance on a more expansive instrumental palette have allowed what was always there to emerge more plainly, from the Celtic harp inspirations to the Appalachian allusions, and, yes, a little bit country. The centerpiece title cut argues best for this successful evolution in a progressive context, beginning with her unabashed plucked intro and mysterious airs, while "Leaving the City" among others sports her evolution into rapid-fire meters, even if the end of the closer is an overly over the top example. Other standouts are the earthier "The Things I say" and "Same Old Man", the earworm "You will not take my heart alive", and especially "A Pin-Light Bent", which sounds like Joanna guesting on an early IAMTHEMORNING number, that is, sublime.While Joanna isn't ever for the musically unadventurous chart gazers, "Divers" is probably the best place to get your feet wet before plunging deeper with abandon, an activity I fully endorse.
items._genre: progressive folk / avant-garde / baroque pop / chamber folk
items._cn_summary: 乐评认为这是乔安娜·纽瑟姆至今最易入耳的一张，但仍保留其核心怪诞气质。与此前作品相比，她的唱法经过调整，歌曲结构更接近常规，配器色彩更开阔，使凯尔特竖琴的根源、阿巴拉契亚音乐的指涉和轻微乡村味道更清晰地浮现。同名开场曲以直率的拨弦和神秘气息成为这场演进的例证；《离开城市》等曲展示出她转向快速音节的能力，但结尾曲尾声有些过度堆砌。其他亮点包括更质朴的《我所言之事》和《同一个老男人》，《你无法活捉我的心》旋律抓人，而《一束针光》尤其突出，像是她客串于某支前卫民谣乐队的早期作品，质感超脱。对于尚未深入其体系的听者，这张专辑是合适的入水处，也为继续向更深处聆听提供了入口。

items.body: Review by tupan — I am not much of a review guy, but after listening to the fourth VISCERA/// album several times, I think I need to give my two cents! VISCERA/// (yep, the three slashes are part of the name) is a italian band that began its career playing grindcore/goregrind in the early 00's, but soon moving to atmospheric sludge in their debut. This one is their fourth full lenght (don't counting two collaboration albums), and was released this year by Time to Kill Records. The music is a refreshing mix of atmo sludge, grunge, prog and many nods to post-punk from the eighties. The vocals change from harsh black metal shrieks to clean Jaz Coleman (from KILLING JOKE fame) inspired singing! I really recommend this album, one of the best surprises of 2026. Check it out!
items._genre: experimental metal / post-metal / atmospheric sludge / post-punk / progressive
items._cn_summary: 意大利乐队VISCERA///的第四张全长专辑，由Time to Kill Records发行。音乐在氛围泥浆金属的基础上，融合了垃圾摇滚、前卫摇滚与八十年代后朋克元素，形成一种层次丰富的声响。人声在黑色金属式尖啸与类似Killing Joke主唱Jaz Coleman的清晰演唱之间切换，增添了戏剧性与张力。专辑整体呈现出粗粝而具实验性的气质，在重型音乐框架内探索了多种风格交汇的可能性，对于偏好实验与前卫方向的听众而言具有吸引力。

items.body: In the spring, Eric van Wonterghem returned with a new album from his Monolith project—the sonic alter ego he launched nearly thirty years ago. For the first time, he is releasing a Monolith album on his own label. Yama is the Hindu god of death and justice, responsible for administering justice and punishing sinners; this theme inspired the album’s ten tracks, at least in the digital version. Monolith remains true to the unique and instantly recognizable sound van Wonterghem has cultivated over the years. It is a precise fusion of Tribal rhythms, Industrial sounds, and Trance-like build-ups. The album as a whole—especially the harder tracks—is highly driving and danceable, culminating in a genuine Trance climax. At the same time, calmer, more atmospheric tracks provide welcome variety while still making a distinct impact on the listener. This is largely due to the remarkable atmosphere Monolith creates once again. Another essential element of the project’s signature sound is the Eastern vibe that permeates the tracks and fits the album’s concept perfectly. Eric van Wonterghem remains a true sound guru, particularly when it comes to the icy tones he weaves into his loops. I am also completely captivated by the deep, overwhelming and explosive bass sounds that anchor the tracks and pair perfectly with the driving rhythms. Monolith has never let me down. This Belgian pioneer once more manages to amaze and convince me. In short, another unmissable album. (Rating:8½). Listen to “Shiva”: Shiva by Monolith About Monolith Monolith is the solo project of Belgian musician Eric van Wonterghem, set up in 1997. Van Wonterghem has also worked with Absolute Body Control, The Klinik, Insekt, Sonar, and Detune-X, and has contributed to Dive album productions. The project built its reputation on a Tribal-Industrial sound, a fusion of Tribal percussion, Industrial production, and Trance-style builds that van Wonterghem has continued to refine across more than a decade of releases. In 2016, Monolith released the four-track EP “Time Running Out” (“Construct”, “De-construct”, “Ghost Cities”, and “Time”) on Sonic Groove, later issued on vinyl. The project also runs its own Bandcamp imprint, SoundOfMonolith, used in 2020 to self-release “The Disco Buddha Variations”, new edits of a track van Wonterghem has described as one of his best-known pieces. Van Wonterghem released his eleventh Monolith album, “Unnatural Bodies”, on Hands in 2020, describing the record as an attempt to make “art without rules” inspired by the mechanical-organic sculptures of artist Jim Whiting. He discussed the approach in a 2020 interview with Side-Line. “Yama”, released on van Wonterghem’s own label Prodam Records, is the first Monolith album issued through his own imprint. The digital edition holds ten tracks built around the album’s theme, the Hindu god of death and justice.
items._cn_summary: 比利时音乐人Eric van Wonterghem以Monolith之名发行新专辑《Yama》，概念取自印度教死神与正义之神雅玛，数字版含十首曲目。专辑延续其数十年来的标志性声音，将部落节奏、工业音色与迷 trance 式渐进结构相融合。东方氛围贯穿全作，与专辑主题高度契合；冰冷的合成器loop、深沉厚重的低音与强劲的鼓机节奏相互锚定。部分偏硬曲目极具冲击力与舞池能量，部分氛围曲目则提供呼吸空间与情绪层次。这是Monolith首张由艺术家自有厂牌Prodam Records发行的专辑，标志其创作自主性的进一步提升。整体制作精致，概念完整，是该系列风格的成熟延续。

items.body: The mind protects itself by hiding what it cannot yet bear to see. Trauma may become a locked room whose very door triggers fear. Denial, dissociation, and avoidance are not proof of hidden programming, but ways consciousness narrows around pain until, with safety, the forbidden room can be approached again. Planeswalkers begin their odyssey with an unusually literal name. The collaboration between gothic songstress Arden Leigh and electronic composer Andrew Means takes its title from the occult idea of moving consciousness between planes through dreams, trance, meditation, astral projection, or other altered states. Their debut EP, The Mind Room, turns that metaphysical vocabulary toward trauma, dissociation, memory, and recovery, imagining the psyche as a series of sealed chambers approached indirectly when direct confrontation feels overwhelming. The record’s premise draws on Leigh’s belief that extreme trauma can create psychological “tripwires,” while denial and avoidance may become forms of protection. Such language carries obvious clinical and spiritual complications, yet The Mind Room is most persuasive when it translates those ideas into texture and movement rather than explanation. Leigh describes the partnership in explicitly occult terms: “Andrew is a really skilled psychic, one of the best I’ve ever met, and he predicted that we’d have more success with it this way. I got a third-party divination just to be sure, and sure enough, it said he was right. We decided to name ourselves Planeswalkers after our shared occult hobbies…I’d say Andrew is a lot better at planeswalking than I am, but I get the job done when needed, or I compensate for it with other aspects of my practice. There were times when we’d finish working on music and then lie down on my floor and astral project together. It’s a really amazing gift to have met someone who shares my two main interests of music and magick like that, and I’m really looking forward to seeing how we continue to explore both of them as we keep working together.” Across four tracks, The Mind Room treats psychic exploration as both subject and compositional principle. The rooms keep changing shape, and the record’s deepest question remains simple: how does someone approach what the mind has placed behind a locked door? Horizons opens amid static, distant electronics, and gentle cymbals. Leigh’s voice floats high above the arrangement with an Enya-like purity, making the track resemble a guided meditation intercepted by an unstable transmission. Its spacious trip-hop architecture recalls Massive Attack, though ruptures of noise repeatedly disturb the calm. Clockwork gives the EP firmer physical dimensions. Leigh’s commanding register suggests Zola Jesus, while Means bends electronic tones into an uncanny interior where corridors seem to extend past their logical endpoints. Repetition becomes claustrophobic, and the title begins to feel mechanical in the psychological sense: a mind caught inside patterns that continue moving after conscious control has weakened. Body makes the sharpest turn. Trip-hop drums support a leering chant, voices push toward shouting, and the earlier inward drift acquires force. The lyric about “walking the planes” supplies the duo with their name, but the song remains intensely corporeal, concerned with breath, rhythm, threat, and will. The closing Alive returns to open space and echo, with Leigh’s voice receding and reappearing as though consciousness were adjusting to gravity after an excursion elsewhere. Order The Mind Room here and listen below: “For resources on plurality, including traumagenic DID, or to make a donation, we recommend supporting The Plural Association here,” suggest the band. Follow Planeswalkers: Instagram YouTube The post Gothic Electronic Duo Planeswalkers Unlock the Psyche on Debut EP “The Mind Room” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: Planeswalkers由哥特女声Arden Leigh与电子作曲家Andrew Means组成，首张EP《The Mind Room》以四首作品探索心灵创伤、解离与记忆恢复的主题，将意识的多个层次喻为封闭的房间，需在安全的条件下逐步接近。创作理念深受两位音乐人的神秘学实践影响，融合冥想、星体投射、占卜等元素。音乐层面，开篇曲在静态噪音与遥远电子声中展开，呈现出类似Enya的空灵人声与Massive Attack式的trip-hop空间感，同时被突如其来的噪音撕裂；第二首加入更扎实的物理感，Leigh的声线让人联想到Zola Jesus，Means的电子音色营造出走廊不断延伸的不安空间，重复节奏制造出心理层面的幽闭感。整张EP将心理学概念转化为声音纹理与动态结构，而非停留在文字层面的解释。

items.body: We were looking forward to being able to talk on the podcast this week about the Diavol Strain set we caught on Sunday, however that won’t be the case. After an apparently awful border crossing into the US the Chilean duo understandably opted not to cross into Canada, as doing so would of course necessitate another entry into the US. Us not getting to see the band behind arguably the year’s best goth record thus far is obviously a drop in the ocean in comparison to larger inconveniences, threats, and acts of violence and murder committed by the current US administration, but it’s a reminder that fascism wants to keep people apart, wants to deny us the opportunity to meet with and learn from those from other parts of the world. You don’t need us to say it, but fuck ICE, fuck white supremacy, fuck everything and everyone related to this atrocity of an American government. Divider Kontravoid, “Without” Oh shit, new Kontravoid incoming. One of the hardest working (and at this point most influential) darkwave acts has been on a tear for a couple of years, with successive banger releases that border on harder industrial, pure synthpop and may other sounds. “Without” continues that trend, with Cam Findlay stretching himself vocally in ways we’ve not yet heard on the new cut, especially on the double-time chorus. Anthemic stuff, and a fine harbinger of what’s to come on October 2nd. Sound of the Void by Kontravoid Dark Chisme, “Suffer Like Me” Seattle’s darkwave duo Dark Chisme has been building their audience the old-fashioned way: by releasing good music, and kicking rich amounts of ass live every time the roll through town. It’s been a real pleasure to watch first hand, especially on their recent show opening up for Omar Doom here in Vancouver where they tore it up on all their established songs, and also tossed this new one “Suffer Like Me” into the mix, which unsurprisingly went over just as well as any other cut they played. Loving the little hints of NRG and freestyle making their way into their sound here, and very keen to hear them continue in this vein in the lead-up to their next album. Suffer Like Me by Dark Chisme Synapscape, “Melting” We’ve had a lot of fun tracking Philipp Münch as he’s dodged down ever odder alleyways over the last few years, from wilfully naive synthpop to oddball dark electro, but a reconvening with Tim Kniep for the project which first brought him international attention is always welcome. Plenty of familiar core elements from across Synapscape’s legacy of powernoise jump out on this teaser from The Future, but the polyrhythmic density which builds up and spirals outward beneath Münch’s restless yowl pushes the envelope quite pleasantly. the future by synapscape Divider, “Nought Point Zero (Portion Control Remix)” Divider’s Zero has been one of the most enjoyable EBM releases of the year, showing how much can be wrought from a little bit of structural experimentation while still holding to no-frills and hard-hitting sound design. Sounds a little like modern day PorCon, no? It’s not surprising, then, to hear how easily a Portion Control bassline can be welded to the moonlit junkyard ambience of the original version of this cut from that record. Nought Point Zero by Divider Silent EM, “Survive (Luminance Remix)” Silent EM isn’t exactly striking while the iron’s hot with a remix LP coming out nearly two full years since the release of Real Life, but a list of contributors including Ortrotasce, Inhalt, Qual, Kontravoid, and Un Hombre Solo brings a lot of star power to this better late than never comp. In particular, the mix of dreamy ghostliness and precise electro pulses on this mix from Brussels-based Luminance is what’s really jumping off the page at us. Silent EM – Real Life (Remixes) by No. Nothing. Never. Records SØLVE, “Nothing Lasts” As is tradition, Brant Showers has released a song on his Birthday as a pay what you want single on Bandcamp. In this case, the song in question is a cover of Matthew Sweet’s “Nothing Lasts”, a classic bit of pop-rock melancholia from the beloved by those who know Girlfriend LP. Far from taking the song into the territory of his usual post-witchhouse ritual dark ambience, Showers plays it straight, amping the spare original into a shoegazey alsice of orchestral pop. Unexpected and absolutely lovely. NOTHING LASTS by SØLVE The post Tracks: September 8th, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: Dungeon synth, the offspring of '90s black metal and ambient music, is a lo-fi genre with a focus on fantastical settings and sonic themes. Ambient music is exactly how it sounds and needs no in-depth explanation for music enthusiasts, and the same attitude extends to the 1990s concrete wave of black metal. Comfy synth, one of numerous prefix-synth sister genres, concentrates on sentimentality and nostalgic sounds; a comfy atmosphere with finite overlap with metal. Comfy synth is a relatively new style, rising in the late 2010s—arguably with Grandma's Cottage's self-titled record, released in December 2019—while dungeon synth falls many decades back. The man behind Hole Dweller, Tim Rowland is a true synth pioneer. Situated in Atlanta, he brought dungeon-infused comfy synth to the ([extremely] relative) mainstream with 2019's Flies the Coop, completing a trilogy started in 2024. His most recent album, Long Road Home, caught my eye this week—mostly through the album art, but partially because of the online hubbub surrounding it. At a digestible half-hour runtime, it isn't a daunting introduction to the genre. Each of the fourteen tracks spans no longer than two minutes (the longest, "stay while the birds sing," reaches 2:47, while "painted in memory" only runs to 1:33), and this is on purpose: Rowland focuses on minimalism, and each track can be looped, like video game soundtracks. Other instruments, like a stringed folk guitar of sorts, are welcome, frequenting tracks with rain and/or nature sounds. The darkest highlight is "bones consumed by moss and root," which takes a badass title and turns the mood to melancholic instead of hopeful. That being said, there are some instances where the focus is taken slightly away from the pure ambience that Hole Dweller convinced me to love in just one playthrough. One is the soft percussion in "summer inventory," and while a steady beat isn't an awful inclusion, the song following it, "sleeping fields," exemplifies that soft cinematics are better on their own, and "in the afterglow" follows this trend. The only other gripe I have is the shift from lo-fi to modern production means. The LP's overall quality dips during "grace in low places" and "in the afterglow", and—despite it being in dungeon synth's nature to not sound crystal clear—the bulk of Long Road Home seems very present-day. This isn't even a complaint though, really, since this duality of feels is perfect for introductory dungeon synthers. Personally, I need no further convincing to join Hole Dweller on the Long Road Home. Long Road Home by Hole Dweller

items.body: Laurie Osborne (Appleblim) describes Liminal Tides with a series of antinomies: awake / asleep, self / no self, and conscious / unconscious mind / no-mind. To these, one could add Bristol / Berlin. It’s no secret that Osborne has spent much of his career as Appleblim between these two cities. While he picked up the mantle Appleblim in London, DJing early dubstep at the foundational FWD>> clubnights, he began producing the stuff upon moving to Bristol in 2006. Bristol is also where his two record labels got their start: Skull Disco (2005-2008) which he ran with Sam Shackelton, and the solo imprint Apple Pips (2008-present, though largely inactive since 2013). At the same time Appleblim got big in Berlin, Ricardo Villalobos and the rest of the minimal techno crowd taking to the unique strain of dubstep pushed by Skull Disco. And soon after Brexit, Appleblim relocated to Berlin, where he teaches synthesis at Catalyst and composes music, both at home ‘in the box’ and at a Funkhaus studiospace shared between friends. Even still, Osborne retains links to Bristol, for instance, as one half of the acclaimed Wrecked Lightship project with Bristolian Adam Winchester. All this to say that Liminal Tides sounds like an oceanic midway point between Bristol and Berlin. The album is filled with all gaseous drums and translucent tides of texture, a triple-point between the more hauntological side of post-post-dubstep (artists like fellow Bristol-to-Berlin producer and Sneaker Social Club signee Low End Activist come to mind) that channels the 1990s doyens of Berlin dub techno. The album begins with “Gaseous,” a birdsong field recording looped and rolled out over chorused dub pads, Monolake’s Hongkong emptied of people and half-returned to the jungle. Appleblim reflects on his love of birdsong, mentioning in a label Q&A how slowing down bird calls draws out their natural glissandos and sonic density that usually lie beyond the limits of human perception—certainly a ‘quiet detail’ if there ever was one. “Warmth” slings out a spindly but still implacably British breakbeat, something that can also be dredged warm and flickering from the depths of “Globule.” The two most percussive tracks, “Crow Crag” and “Weather Vane,” arrive next Both are driving but in the style of tape hiss-drenched somnambulant fugues rather than being dancefloor ready. The tracks represent dub techno annealed with dubsteppy low-end density and melodic experimentation; the former track layers in bits of Tangerine Dream-esque arpeggiation while chimes punctuate the latter like hypnic jerks. “Seagull” closes the set, the closest thing to a conventional ambient track built almost entirely from a swirling foghorn sample laced with seagull cries. This return to the water and air binds together the cycle of life, of which Liminal Tides’ antimonies are only a part of a coherent whole. (Marcello Ursic)
items._genre: dub techno / ambient / post-dubstep / field recording
items._cn_summary: Appleblim的《Liminal Tides》以一系列对立概念构建：清醒与沉睡、自我与无我、有意识与无意识，加上布里斯托与柏林两座城市之间的游牧状态。专辑融合了气体般的鼓机声效与半透明的质感洪流，介于后后dubstep的灵异美学与九十年代柏林dub techno之间。开场曲《Gaseous》以循环鸟鸣录音搭配合唱dub pad，灵感来自Monolake的空旷空间与丛林回归；《Warmth》与《Globule》呈现英式breakbeat的纤细脉络；《Crow Crag》与《Weather Vane》以磁带嘶声包裹的梦游式赋格推进，融合Tangerine Dream式琶音与钟声碎片；终曲《Seagull》几乎完全由雾号采样与海鸥叫声编织而成，构成最接近传统ambient的篇章。整张专辑是一次关于中间地带的声音冥想，将自然录音、电子质感与节奏实验熔铸为连贯的循环。

items.body: That Porous Line follows as a deliberate shift—letting in just enough light to see differently without abandoning the dark corners they prefer to inhabit. Push For Night arrives here as a natural fit That Porous Line by Push For Night   Room40 has been one of experimental music’s most important and quietly consistent labels since Lawrence English founded it in Brisbane in 2000. Over 25 years and more than 300 releases, it has built a catalog that spans electroacoustic composition, musique concrète, ambient, and avant-garde sound art—releasing work from Ben Frost, Tujiko Noriko, William Basinski, Grouper, and dozens of others. English works from a home studio built beneath a storage room containing literally a ton of records, an apt metaphor for a label that operates under the weight of its own history while continuing to push forward. Push For Night arrives here as a natural fit.​ The duo of Oliver Chapoy—Brooklyn-based musician, producer, and engineer known for his work with Saxon Shore, Warm Ghost, and collaborations with Helado Negro and Mikael Jorgensen of Wilco and James Elliott, Louisville, KY-based and equally steeped in experimental and post-rock sensibility, began their collaboration in 2017 and have been slowly building a body of work that lives at the intersection of electroacoustic processing, collage, and abstract sound construction. Their previous Room40 release Lapsed Gasps was a dense, intense record built around Jon Mueller‘s archived percussion recordings, processed through heavy electronics. That Porous Line follows as a deliberate shift—letting in just enough light to see differently without abandoning the dark corners they prefer to inhabit. “It’s Sure To Be Dark If You Shut Your Eyes” is a standout. The drums and glitched phaser of what sounds like a rolling percussion or hit every 8 to 16 bars is beautiful to the ear. There is a lot of stereo panning at play with their sound elements throughout, and while there really isn’t any persistent melody taking place, this leans more toward sound play and effects stacking—how many effects can they layer onto the same overlying loop until it gets absolutely destroyed and becomes something else. That question is the compositional engine driving a lot of this album, and here it’s applied with precision rather than aggression. “Idler’s Reward” is another strong one as far as melodic content goes—its emotional build and three-part structure make it a compelling standpoint for emotional construction. The song has three distinct sections if you hear it that way. What sounds like a marking drum echoing in the background is ringed with delay and echo on particular instruments and synths, making it interesting to listen to as it unfolds. Right at the six-minute mark, a highpass filter is applied to a looping note being echoed as a beautiful clarinet, played by Zachary Koeber—emerges as the second section of the track, playing out until 7:39 where the third section arrives with no warning: distorted, filtered guitar chords coming in and echoing to their own death. It is a fascinating build piece that earns every minute of its eight-plus-minute runtime. “Bait Is Lowered” continues the album’s definition of itself as a collection of building emotional pieces. Another fascinating piece of sounds. The incredible thing about experimental ambience like this is how long you can keep the listener engaged with the sounds being created and fatiguing them with noise or drone. Halfway through this track there’s a disruption—what can only be described as if you took a drum beat and submerged it in a bucket of water and started washing it aggressively as it builds up with suds. The music is very much imaginative. “Turned Slowly And Slowly Turned” is another dark piece with very subtle coos and creaky electronic rolls simulating what sounds like electronic animals or chirps, separated into two distinctive zones, far away and reverbed out on one side, the subtle coos chirping consistently back and forth softly on the other, no effects on them but slowed. Distortion play at its finest. “Push For Night describes their process as decorating the cave and inviting specters to reveal a message, trying to catch something in the semi-dark.” ~J. Batista “That Porous Line” is actually a beautiful closer, not the one expected after listening to this piece, but one that sounds genuinely immersive. The concept and theme of the album is still present, the bizarre distortions remain, but the melodies are toned down. Towards the end of the track there may be recycled field recordings surfacing, not to the naked ear but the trained one would catch it. The overall listen is actually pleasing, which for Push For Night is itself a notable statement. This is fundamentally an effects album and it shows, in the best possible way. The structure of experimentation with guitars and ambience has come a long way from the post-rock tradition that both Chapoy and Elliott carry in their backgrounds, and what That Porous Line represents is those backgrounds fully dissolved into something that no longer resembles where it came from. Push For Night describes their process as decorating the cave and inviting specters to reveal a message, trying to catch something in the semi-dark. On That Porous Line, they caught more than they usually let go of, and the result is their most emotionally varied and accessible work yet, which for this duo still means strange, flickering, and lit by crepuscular light. That’s the appeal. That Porous Line is available on Room40. [Bandcamp] That Porous Line by Push For NightThe post Push For Night :: That Porous Line (Room40) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Push For Night组合在Room40厂牌下的新作，由Brooklyn音乐人Oliver Chapoy与Louisville的James Elliott组成，他们的合作始于2017年，作品横跨电声处理、拼贴与抽象声音构建。专辑延续了前作Lapsed Gasps对密集电子处理的探索，但做出了方向性调整——让光线适度进入，保留黑暗质感的同时改变了听觉视角。专辑的核心创作逻辑围绕着一个问题展开：在同一循环上叠加多少效果，直到它被彻底破坏并转化为另一种事物。立体声摆位手法丰富，虽然缺乏持续旋律，但作品更偏向声音游戏与效果堆叠。开篇曲It’s Sure To Be Dark If You Shut Your Eyes展现了打击乐碎片与相位失真器的结合，Idler’s Reward则以三段式结构构建情感递进，六分钟处的高通滤波器揭开单簧管演奏的层次。单簧管由Zachary Koeber演奏，与回声中的鼓声交织，形成耐听的展开感。

items.body: Guitar in jazz. A strange beast, with which we had some issues coming to terms for a long time. In "traditional" jazz (with all the limitations of that adjective, but you get it), it passed us by almost unnoticed. Sure, Django Reinhardt, Wes Montgomery, Charlie Christian et al: legends to whom we bow, but, to be honest, they slipped away without leaving any deep or meaningful trace. We’re sorry, respectfully sorry: our fault. Far more interesting is the contribution of guitars in Miles' electric turn, while the super virtuoso sounds of the likes of Pat Metheny or John Scofield left us emotionally inert. As soon as the instrument becomes edgy and menacing, it begins to win us over, Sonny Sharrock, James Blood Ulmer first, then Arto Lindsay, Thurston Moore, Jim O'Rourke, Bill Orcutt, Keiji Haino are the names. The sharper, the better. In our own actual Valhalla, that sees Derek Bailey as the Supreme Odin, recently entered (becoming a sick obsession) Masayuki Takayanagi, a guilty belated epiphany of ours, and guitars as improper weapons take us with the guard down, unable to offer any resistance. The current free/improv scene is quite a golden vein, offering guitars for every taste, just head over to the dedicated section of our forum and you could dig in a six-string bonanza until your hands bleed. With Ava Mendoza, whatever the line-up on the field (alone, collaborations, groups), the turntable spins by itself and the moment to quit declaring our boundless love for her, as we did in previous reviews, is still far away. The reason? Very simple: it could be in disguise of country, metal or noise but she's got THE blues. We're obviously talking about the dirty, kind-of-black, hooch-flavored one that inhabits the rosters of Fat Possum and In The Red Records, the spleen of Jeffrey Lee Pierce, the fury of Nick Cave's, pre-Gucci loafers, Birthday Party, the desperation of Alan Vega's solo albums or the hyper saturated textures of Mick Collins’ bands. Did you say Attitude? Ava not only has it, but she proved, with the astonishing Mama Killa project, to be able to cross the Shadow Line, to venture into the Heart of Darkness, coming back to tell all about it. Natural. Gifted. The new album, recorded live in Antwerp, Madison, Chicago and Firenze, features the Brooklyn-based musician reinterpreting seven songs from her "New Spell" and "Circular Train" records, along with a new composition, "Mama Cocha”. The recipe is the one we know and love: fuzz, harmonic progressions, solos and distortions are the facets of a virtuosic prism that's never self-referential or an end in itself, but always in service of the Ultimate Ideal: the Blues. The "togetherness" side of the work sees Ava joined by Maestro Hamid Drake, adding his sparse yet extraordinary polyrhythms on four tracks, demonstrating once more, that, as Voltaire said, "les grands esprits se rencontrent." Another solid hit from Phil Freeman's label, whose production portfolio is beginning to take on a truly interesting and relevant profile: long may the Ambulance burn. Alive Alone, Alive Together by Ava Mendoza Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑收录了吉他手Ava Mendoza在安特卫普、麦迪逊、芝加哥和佛罗伦萨的现场录音，重新演绎了她此前专辑中的七首作品并加入新曲。她以模糊失真、复杂和声进行与密集独奏构建音乐，风格跨越乡村、金属与噪音，但始终贯穿一种粗粝、深沉、近乎黑色的布鲁斯血脉。鼓手Hamid Drake在四首作品中加入稀疏而精妙的复合节奏层，与Mendoza形成呼应。整张作品强调现场的即时性与即兴张力，不追求技术炫耀，而是将失真吉他作为表达原始情感的工具，在噪音与布鲁斯之间找到独特的平衡点。
