items.body:
The brotherhood of foundational European avant garde bassists gets smaller with each passing year. And among those still living, some are either inactive for various reasons or working in other fields, musical or otherwise. So, the subset of ones still going is a small but precious list.

Among them is the Netherlands’ Arjen Gorter. Ask even a relatively informed listener of European avant garde jazz about him and almost invariably the first association will be Willem Breuker, and more specifically his Kollektief. Gorter did anchor that group for the entirety of its existence (1975-2010, with a retrospective farewell tour coming after Breuker’s death) alongside drummer Rob Verdurmen, allowing Breuker and a rotating cast of string and horn players (though trombonist Bernard Hunnekink was another stalwart) to navigate complex and subversive music, confident that a strong foundation would always support them. But like Jimmy Cobb always being referenced first and sometimes only as the last living participant of Kind of Blue after Miles Davis died in 1991, Gorter’s career, still ongoing, is hardly exclusive to his work with Breuker.

Gorter was born in Amsterdam on January 2nd, 1948 and he has resided in the Dutch capital his whole life. His road to the bass was a circuitous one. As he wrote in an email, “I liked the accordion when I was very young. It was common in the Amsterdam streets of the ‘50s, but the tunes that my teacher made me play were too silly, so that did not last. My dad imported musical instruments. He brought a slightly damaged ukulele home and so at around 11 I tried playing along with the nightly jazz broadcasts on French and Belgian radio. The father of a friend had a small jazz collection and I loved the Art Blakey Blue Note 45s, the Monk LP and the other stuff he had. So that ukulele was replaced by a guitar. I started jamming in our attic with friends and others and at some point someone brought a double bass upstairs and left it there for six months. I had fun playing it and managed to buy it from him once he showed up again.”

During high school Gorter played guitar in a band for school dances, repertoire ranging from period rock tunes to jazz compositions. He began college in 1966, aiming to study political science and sociology, the same year he first worked professionally with Breuker, having heard the older reed player’s bands around town and once playing with him at a jam session. Gorter was invited to join a new Breuker group, which performed at the Loosdrecht Jazz Competition as a sextet, then expanded to almost two-dozen musicians for the final stage. This group would make Litany for the 14th of June 1966 (Relax) in late October 1966, Gorter’s recording debut alongside two other bassists, the much older Dick van der Capellen and Victor Kaihatu.

Gorter would balance university and performing for a few years. During this time, he would work with Germany’s Gunter Hampel, appearing on his April 1968 Wergo date Gunter Hampel Group + Jeanne Lee and participating in the November 1968 Total Music Meeting in Berlin, where photo evidence has him in a bizarre encounter with Hampel, John McLaughlin, Sonny Sharrock, Pharoah Sanders, Roy Ayers, Laurie Allan, and Roel Kroes. 1969 saw even more activity: more Hampel work, including the album The 8th of July 1969 (inaugurating his Birth imprint); playing on German trumpeter Manfred Schoof’s FMP release European Echoes and being part of the Peter Brötzmann Oktett at the International Holy Hill Jazz Meeting (alongside Buschi Niebergall and Peter Kowald; Richard Williams’ review of European Echoes in the March 14th, 1970 issue of Melody Maker saying, “It’s an astonishingly powerful performance, with particularly superb work by Dudek, Bailey and the three basses, who play a really fantastic trio section.”). Gorter is also heard on the Live at The Bohemia Jazzclub recording by Hans Dulfer’s Soulbrass Inc., as well as a track with Breuker and Han and Peter Bennink heard on the Instant Composers Pool cheese box. As Gorter recalled, “I managed to juggle both activities until the end of 1969, but I was more on the road than in Amsterdam and had to make a choice and I chose the activity that gave me way more satisfaction.”

During the first half of the ‘70s, Gorter and Breuker did not work together often, at least as can be gleaned from available recordings: Hampel’s People Symphony (Birth, 1970) and part of his group that participated in German avant garde composer Hans Werner Henze’s Der Langwierige Weg In Die Wohnung Der Natascha Ungeheuer; and an unofficial Amsterdam recording from 1973 under Breuker’s leadership and a live date from Leo Cuypers in 1974, both with groups prefiguring the Kollektief (Cuypers was its first pianist). Otherwise Gorter was busy – again, at least on record – with Hans Dulfer, Kees Hazevoet, Theo Loevendie, Alexander Von Schlippenbach, and the Irène Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl Quartet. The latter two were significant. Gorter was part of the second iteration of Schlippenbach’s Globe Unity Orchestra, Niebergall and Kowald in tow once more (a 1970 Berlin Jazz Festival performance released in 2001) and the Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl group that was active for several years. “I met Rudiger in Wuppertal, that was a new jazz center by itself thanks to Peter Brötzmann and Peter Kowald,” wrote Gorter. “Sometimes I stayed at the studio that he shared with guitar wizard Hans Reichel. When Irene and Rudiger started playing together, they asked me to join and we played many places in the early ‘70s, with Heinrich Hock, Louis Moholo, or Alan Bateman on drums.” That band made only one full album, 1974’s Goose Pannée (FMP) but did have a track on the For Example - Workshop Freie Musik 1969 - 1978, the FMP boxed set.

1974-75 was an important period for two other reasons. Besides the aforementioned collaborations as well as work with the Boy Edgar Big Band and the small groups of Maurice Horsthuis and Toon van Vliet, Gorter was one of the musicians who helped establish Amsterdam’s Bimhuis, ultimately one of Europe’s premier venues for avant garde music, performing on its October 1st, 1974 opening night with the Burton Greene Quartet. Then in March 1975, Breuker asked Gorter to be a member of his Kollektief. Gorter described the group’s music as such: “Willem’s music had a lot of freedom. There were often tightly arranged written sections that would suddenly end and then the fun was to play on as if the arrangement continued – there was usually no such thing as chord changes – or to let the thing fall off a cliff ... Anyway, the music always felt fresh to play, even after many concerts, and there was a great mix of individual input and group discipline and cooperation. The Kollektief’s music linked the recognizable to the unexpected, often in 90-degree turns. It was surprising but accessible. For us musicians there was a wide spectrum of activities, from theater plays to movie music to interpretations of classical music and a lot of traveling to places where we found appreciative audiences, ranging from Australian school children to Chinese businessmen.”

The Kollektief would go on to make over three dozen albums, mostly released on Breuker’s BV Haast label, and perform all over the world, including during the Klap op de Vuurpijl (roughly, Top It All Off) Festival, taking place over five days at the end of each year from 1976-2005. Its book mixed Breuker and other band member pieces with tunes from various pages of the Great American Songbook and drawn from the classical canon, as well as other sources, presented in a highly theatrical manner best appreciated live and mixing in humor in refreshing contrast to the dour stage demeanor of many an improviser.

As busy as the Kollektief would keep him, Gorter still pursued other projects, some including fellow Kollektief members, including Breuker, and only existing on stages, such as groups under the leadership of Maarten van Norden, Sean Bergin, Boy Raaymakers, Pierre Courbois, Nedly Elstak, Jasper van ‘t Hof, Misha Mengelberg, and others. A representative sampling of those can be found in the archive of the Bimhuis (https://www.bimhuis.nl/archief); when he was in Amsterdam, this would be Gorter’s home near his home.

But there were also ones documented as albums: Maine, the 1975 collaboration of American trombonist Roswell Rudd with Dulfer, Gorter, and drummer Martin van Duynhoven, was made up of music by Sonny Rollins and Rudd (who had been coming to and working in the Netherlands since the mid ‘60s both with the New York Art Quartet and also locals like Loevendie). There were two 1977 dates by Cuypers, Zeeland Suite also including another bassist in South African expatriate Harry Miller; the 1979 Maarten Van Norden/Boy Raaymakers quartet date Chicken Song, completed by drummer Peter Nykyruj (of Mike Osborne fame); and a pair of 1980 albums spearheaded by the aforementioned trumpeter/composer Elstak (and released on his Coreco label; Gorter had loosely studied harmony with him in the ‘60s): To Build was led by Soesja Citroen’s name, who was one of five singers alongside Elstak, Breuker, Gorter, and Van Duynhoven for Sad Trumpets. The most significant, at least in terms of international exposure, came in July 1984, when Gorter, Mengelberg, and Bennink joined forces with two Americans, soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy and trombonist George Lewis, for the Soul Note release Change of Season (Music Of Herbie Nichols). Another important recording came 13 years later with Legendary: The 27th of May 1997, in a reunion with Hampel, who was fêting his seminal Heartplants SABA album from 1965 with original participants Courbois, Schlippenbach, and Schoof, Gorter standing in for his late friend Buschi Niebergall. One interesting takeaway from this is that it is often thought that after Breuker split with his fellow Instant Composers Pool founders Mengelberg and Bennink there were two distinct worlds in Dutch avant garde jazz; however, there were musicians like Gorter who operated in both spheres.

The new millennium found Gorter in several new projects: the mostly American blues/jazz band New Texas Swing from American saxophonist and then fellow Kollektief member Alex Coke with singer Tina Marsh and drummer John Betsch; the aptly named though horn-heavy Drummers Double Bill from Arend Niks and Verdurmen; 2000 recording The Compositions Of Eric Dolphy (BV Haast) with Coke, Breuker, Eric Vloeimans, Frank van Bommel, and John Engels; and Bo Van De Graaf’s I Compani; and the Rahsaan Roland Kirk “tribute” band Reeds & Deeds, also put together by Van De Graaf.

The Dolphy project had a personal resonance for Gorter, more specifically a much younger version of himself. In 1964, when he was 16, Gorter attended the Charles Mingus Sextet performance at Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw, a band with Dolphy, Johnny Coles, Clifford Jordan, Jaki Byard, and Dannie Richmond, which Gorter calls “the best ever ... Halfway through a trumpet solo by Johnny Coles, Eric left the stage while playing and walked into the hall. He ended up right next to my seat, way in the back. For a 16-year-old, that may have been a life-changing experience.” In 2011, Gorter was given the opportunity to celebrate Dolphy once more with a concert at the Bimhuis: “Eric Dolphy at The Five Spot Revisited,” with the legendary recording’s repertoire played by himself, Tom Arthurs, Rudi Mahall/Alex Coke (as his bass clarinet and saxophone/flute sides), Benoît Delbecq, and John Betsch.

Gorter joined the multimedia ensemble I Compani, founded by Van De Graaf in 1985, in 2010. As he wrote, “Bo van de Graaf just called it quits for I Compani, which I understand but regret. He led that band for 40 years through great adventures and I was happy to participate since 2010 or so. If anyone is comparable to Breuker in the amount of initiatives he took, it is him. Original pieces are blended with film music and live video, in various lineups from septet to 18-piece band. His music has the space, freedom and versatility of Breuker’s, but in a different way. Fun!”

When asked about the European scene in which he came up, Gorter replied, “At that time every European city had a very original and recognizable improvised music scene, or a few of them, like London with both the Spontaneous Music Ensemble and Brotherhood of Breath,” he wrote. “And they all had international contacts and were sharing with each other. So, the originality of these approaches, and the mutual respect, encouraged the exchange between countries and scenes and the musicians and their supporters took the initiative to made it happen.”

As for his own methodology towards, as shown in this piece, the variety of musical situations in which he has taken part, Gorter spoke both simply and profoundly: “From the beginning I played both free improvisation and tunes based on chord changes. Learning on stage was an option in the ‘60s, which sometimes led to embarrassment but more often to improvement. My approach is: first try to play what you hear, then figure out what others call it (= music theory), then apply that to play better what you hear and so on. Nowadays much education starts on the second step ...”
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评以荷兰贝斯手Arjen Gorter为焦点，回顾他在欧洲前卫爵士场景中的长期实践，尤其是作为Willem Breuker Kollektief核心成员的经历。文章通过Gorter的自述，讲述了他从幼年接触手风琴、尤克里里到最终转向低音提琴的过程，并交代了他与Breuker的初次合作及录音起点。内容侧重人物生平与音乐脉络梳理，强调Gorter在自由即兴与复杂乐队编制中所提供的稳固低音支撑，同时也点明他并非只与Breuker相关，而是拥有更广泛的音乐活动。对于理解欧洲前卫爵士贝斯手的角色、Breuker团队的运作方式以及60年代荷兰爵士圈的生态，此文提供了有价值的背景信息。文章尚未深入到具体专辑曲目分析，但已勾勒出艺术家在即兴传统中的位置。

items.body: Invisible Island quietly removes itself from the rest of the world. Sonic Pieces return with their first release of a new decade, and the album is also a continuation of 2016’s Minor Planet. Midori Hirano’s restrained and overcast music reflects a Japanese water garden more than a sun-kissed paradise. In fact, the sun doesn’t cast much light at all. Diluted greens replace bright sands as overcast, rainy skies hang over a piano. Hirano’s piano shares the area with a set of lurking electronics, sometimes subtle in their scurrying and sometimes snaking through the undergrowth. Some of the electronics are abrasive, but they’re few and far between, and the watery tones, spreading outwards with a series of rhythmic ripples, are always there to soften the sound. Invisible Island is an album of rhythm, both concealed and obvious, with a gentle, undulating motion underlining the whole experience. Rhythms take the form of repeating piano lines, obtuse electronics, or a dull, continuous thumping – the sound of a heartbeat. Fluctuating drones, warbling and wobbling as if on a stormy lake, help to expand the album. Every tone adds to the record’s exotic flavour, and the music retains a vibe of cool relaxation and sober calm. The introduction of a violin on ‘Belong’ (played by Christoph Berg) keeps everything grounded and stuck in the mud of a lower register. Rainy days can be beautiful, too, and Hirano’s music takes a different approach, the piano rippling outwards and finding its own subdued space. Unfurling like a strange flower, Invisible Island was born in solitude, and its music allows the listener to recharge. Disconnecting from the world and finding a hidden retreat such as this is not only recommended but essential for wellbeing. Invisible Island is out February 7.
items._cn_summary: 《Invisible Island》是 Midori Hirano 在 Sonic Pieces 厂牌发行的专辑，作为2016年《Minor Planet》的延续，延续了阴郁克制的气质。整张专辑以一架钢琴为核心，辅以潜伏的电子音色——有时如低频脉冲般隐现，有时如爬行的藤蔓般蜿蜒，偶尔出现粗糙的电子质感但总体被水润的音色包裹。节奏以多种形态贯穿：重复的钢琴音型、迂回的电子节拍、以及如心跳般的低频律动。浮动的嗡鸣如暴风雨中的湖面般摇曳膨胀，扩展了专辑的空间感。小提琴在《Belong》中的加入将一切锚定于低频泥泞之中。这张专辑在孤独中诞生，其音乐让听者得以重新充电，断开与世界的连接、找到隐藏的庇护所成为必需而非可选项。

items.body: With a picturesque, pastoral centre, Southern Points reclines towards the warmth of the sunshine. Patient and flexible, the latest release from Greg Baird’s Moss Covered Technology project shelters in the safety – and the surrounding beauty – of the countryside: open fields and cresting hills, kissing gates tucked away behind stone walls and leaves blowing in a breeze of scented blossom. Southern Points (Hibernate) hits all the right notes… Sparse, spacious, and introverted, the ambient soundscapes reflect a period of deep introspection for Baird. Choosing to focus on family life and life at home, there’s something very comforting about the tones here: they’re gentle and approachable, with warm smiles lighting up familiar faces. With the use of a Prophet 12, varying effects pedals, and processed field recordings, the soundscapes stretch out and the flowering melodies melt in the light of a Spring sun. The lightest wind wisps by, and heavier, supporting drones hint at a strengthening of the sunlight as an early morning haze turns to the strong musculature of midday. Scenery is crucial to the record, and its beauty was experienced first-hand. Baird is an eye-witness to the wonder of the day, and he translates this slice of peace into the language of music. It all came from a day out, the scenery and nature around him inspiring the creation of the album. Baird’s photos acted as additional inspiration during the writing and creating process. The organic ambient hues help to turn the original image into music…but it goes at a sedate pace, with everything coming to fruition at just the right time, waiting for the right season. The album is warm – but not boiling. Listeners will still need a gilet and a light outer layer, but it’s indicative of Spring’s welcoming touch. Light electronics scrape against the side of a wooden fence. New shoots rise up from the soil; birds begin to chirp; the evenings are lighter for longer. Bursts of lavender colour the fields. The countryside beckons. www.hibernate.bandcamp.com
items._cn_summary: 格雷格·贝尔德以乡间一日为创作起点，将开阔田野、石墙、鸟鸣与春日微风等实地录音，转译为疏朗、温暖而内向的氛围声景。 Prophet 12 合成器、效果器与处理后的环境采样彼此交融，旋律如花朵般缓慢舒展，低沉持续音则提供稳定支撑。作品不追求强烈冲击，而以从容节律、空间感与家庭生活带来的私密气息取胜；其独特之处在于把摄影所见和个人沉思转化为具有鲜明季节感的声音肖像，适合偏好环境声、氛围电子与细致声音设计的听众。

items.body: Christina Vantzou’s sound has been further refined on her fourth album for Kranky – one listen to the opening piece, ‘Glissando for Bodies and Machines in Space’, is enough to leave the listener’s jaw hanging as the piece sets the tone for the rest of the album, a slow pirouette into limitless space, completely lost in the dark pull of an orbit where a lone voice slides and swirls into oblivion. Suspended, spacious and void-like, the composition unravels a darker side, and No. 4 excels at beckoning these smoky shadows into its midst. Something of a monolithic shape, something unseen, is gathering in the gloom. Her ambient and classical music has always favoured the minimal, and No. 4 provides a deeper experience because of it. Once upon a time, her music had more rigidity in its orchestral skeleton, structured while keeping its smooth ambient flow and caress, with lambent harmonies and cinematic drones mirroring her work with Adam Wiltzie as The Dead Texan. Nowadays, her music embraces the experimental and the ephemeral, bridging the gap between the dislocated two and turning what was once disjointed into a cohesive outlet. For Vantzou, No. 4 is an evolution, a new side, a new face standing in the same doorway. At the same time, this face looks familiar, like an old friend seen a decade later. Their phrasing and their fingerprints are the same, and in that respect Vantzou’s music is still recognizable, but it’s morphing, evolving. Vantzou’s ambient drones are still in place, but electronics slither and scuttle around them. ‘At Dawn’ glows with a series of swelling strings, and the deep, processed drones echo forever, surrounding everything with elegant displays. Her music lies on the periphery, like the late-rising dawn or the sunset in the street. No. 4 also features a number of musical collaborations, including Steve Hauschildt, John Also Bennett (Forma), Angel Deradoorian, Clarice Jensen, Beatrijs De Klerck and members of Belgium’s Echo Collective. But Vantzou aimed to ‘blur lines of hierarchy’, so members of the ensemble were allowed to add or delete parts of their own free will, and this has only strengthened the album. Citing sleep and the loosening of time in her private and professional life, Vantzou’s music appears in the form of a dream-like fugue, an endless glint of light rising up from a well of darkness and introspection. www.christinavantzou.bandcamp.com
items._cn_summary: 这是Christina Vantzou在Kranky厂牌发行的第四张专辑，展现了她从早期带有古典骨架的环境音乐向更实验、更飘渺方向的进化。专辑以弦乐、深层处理过的嗡鸣和电子音效为核心，营造出悬空、幽暗且具有电影感的氛围。开场曲在缓慢旋转中将人声引向深渊，整体像一场从黑暗中升起的梦境赋格。专辑邀请了多位合作者参与，包括Steve Hauschildt、John Also Bennett、Angel Deradoorian等，但Vantzou刻意模糊主从关系，让乐手自由增减声部，使作品更具凝聚力。从早期与Adam Wiltzie合作的The Dead Texan那种结构化的管弦乐氛围，到现在拥抱短暂性与实验性，她的音乐在保持辨识度的同时持续蜕变。

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 乐队的这张专辑延续了首作的风格拼贴策略，最显著的特色在于乐器本身：乐队用废弃物品和零碎材料自制了多种非常规乐器，包括tassofons、kitchenofon等古怪命名，在现代录音技术下仍能保持准确的音高和丰富音质。专辑将克莱兹默、昆比亚、桑巴、非洲节拍、中东旋律等多种世界音乐风格编织在一起，每首曲目对应不同的文化灵感来源。乐手在自制限定下展现出扎实的演奏技巧，多首曲目包含即兴段落，跨越节奏进行爵士化的旋律对话。这张作品既是对世界各地音乐传统的致敬，也是对音乐本质的反思：在精工细作的乐器唾手可得的时代，真正的音乐人依然能用垃圾和废料创造出动人的声音。

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Led by its frontman and multi-instrumentalist, Christofer Johnsson, Therion dedicates "Secret of the Runes" (2001), its tenth album, to exploring the mysteries of Yggdrasil: the enormous sacred tree that occupies a central place in the Norse worldview and around which the nine worlds are arranged. The concept is rooted in the fascinating Norse mythology, as transmitted by medieval sources that preserve much older traditions. An album shrouded in the misty, mystical, and legendary aura inspired by gods, giants, humans, and elves, it is grounded in symphonic metal with a distinct neoclassical element and serves as a starting point for delving into the various branches of the metal genre found within the Swedes' broad and shadowy sonic spectrum.Thus, the intricate choral, orchestral, and operatic arrangements of the thirty or so guest musicians blend harmoniously with Kristian Niemann's powerful and sophisticated guitar riffs and solos, both in the death metal elements of the majestic "Ginnungagap" -which opens the way to the chaos of the primordial void of creation and is surely one of the album's best tracks- as well as in the depths of the doom-laden "Jotunheim," the black-metal darkness of the lugubrious "Nifelheim" and "Helheim," and the power-metal-style bursts of energy in the fast-paced "Asgard" and "Muspelheim."And that sense of persistent tension and chaos conveyed by the most extreme and dense tracks finds gradations in the more progressive "Schwarzalbenheim" and a breath of fresh air both in the serene "Midgard" - which refers to the realm of humans and is another of the album's major themes - and in the folk-metal interludes of the celestial "Ljusalfheim" and the pastoral "Vanaheim." All of this comes together to form an album with a wide range of nuances that mesh seamlessly, which the title track "Secret of the Runes" sums up as an operatic compendium and a very fitting concluding epilogue.An excellent album that, along with "Theli" (1996) and "Vovin" (1998), represents one of the highest peaks of compositional and musical maturity in the band's entire career, as well as establishing itself as a cornerstone of symphonic metal.4 stars

items._cn_summary: 专辑以北欧神话中的世界树伊格德雷西尔为概念核心，围绕九个世界展开叙事。音乐上以交响金属为基底，融入死亡金属、厄运、黑金属、力量金属及民谣金属等元素，三十余位客座音乐家参与合唱、管弦与歌剧编排，与吉他演奏形成强烈对比。曲目如《Ginnungagap》展现死亡金属的混沌力量，《Jotunheim》偏向厄运沉郁，《Nifelheim》和《Helheim》带有黑金属的阴暗气质，而《Midgard》等则较为舒缓，标题曲作为歌剧式总结收束全篇。整体在极端与优美之间呈现丰富层次，被视为乐队创作成熟期的代表作品之一。

items.body: Laibach released “WAT” on 8 September 2003 through Mute Records. The album turns 23 this year. Iztok Turk and Laibach produced the record, with Umek co-producing and sharing mixing duties with Turk; Nilesh Patel handled mastering at The Exchange. The track “Anti-Semitism” was separately produced and mixed by Temponauta. “WAT” is an acronym for “We Are Time,” revealed on the title track. Laibach has described the album’s intent as being not about “what Laibach is, or what it wants, but what you are and where you stand.” What is on Laibach’s ‘WAT’ The CD edition runs 12 tracks: “B Mashina”, “Tanz mit Laibach”, “Du bist unser”, “Achtung!”, “Ende”, “Now You Will Pay”, “Hell: Symmetry”, “Das Spiel ist aus”, “Satanic Versus”, “The Great Divide”, “WAT” and “Anti-Semitism”, with a total running time of 58:23. The 2LP vinyl edition replaces “Now You Will Pay” in its track sequence with the bonus cut “Reject or Breed” and runs 62:27. The CD also carries an enhanced video for “Tanz mit Laibach”. Tomi Meglič of Siddharta contributed music, lyrics and additional vocals on “B Mashina”. Long-time NSK collaborator Peter Mlakar wrote lyrics for “Du bist unser” and “Achtung!”. Slavko Avsenik Jr. arranged the choir parts and co-wrote the title track, and Matej Mršnik played guitar on “Ende”. “Tanz mit Laibach” was released as a single on 25 August 2003, with remixes by Umek, Johannes Heil, Zeta Reticula and Temponauta, and an accompanying video directed by Sašo Podgoršek. About Laibach Laibach formed in 1980 in Trbovlje, a mining town in Slovenia, then part of Yugoslavia. The band’s name is the German-language name for Ljubljana, a deliberate reference to the World War II occupation of Slovenia. In December 1984, Laibach co-founded Neue Slowenische Kunst (NSK) alongside the visual-art collective Irwin and the Scipion Nasice Sisters Theatre, uniting music, art and theatre under a single project. The band released its debut album, “Laibach”, in 1985 through the Slovenian label ŠKUC Ropot. From 1987 onward, Laibach recorded primarily for Mute Records, releasing “Krst pod Triglavom – Baptism” and “Opus Dei” in 1987, followed by covers albums “Let It Be” (1988) and “Sympathy for the Devil” (1988/1990). “Kapital” followed in 1992, then “NATO” in 1994, reworking military and pop songs against the backdrop of the Yugoslav wars, and “Jesus Christ Superstars” in 1996, a reinterpretation of the Andrew Lloyd Webber rock opera. “WAT” arrived in 2003, continuing the band’s practice of operating as a collective rather than a fixed lineup. Laibach followed “WAT” with the career-spanning compilation “Anthems” in 2004 and the national-anthem reworking “Volk” in 2006. The band has continued releasing new material into the 2020s, including the symphonic work “Alamut” in 2025 and the studio album “Musick” in 2026.
items._cn_summary: 这张2003年的专辑延续了乐队对权力结构与意识形态的审视，以“我们是时间”为概念核心。声响上融合了工业节拍、电子混音与合唱编排，客座乐手与词曲作者的参与增加了层次感。专辑在制式电子节奏中嵌入戏剧化人声，既有冷硬的机械感，又不乏古典仪式般的庄重。曲目安排紧凑，不同版本之间也存在差异，体现了乐队一贯的集体创作方式。整体上，这是一张具有明确艺术指向的作品，适合对暗潮与工业声响抱有浓厚兴趣的听众。

items.body: For a few years, I have had this funny vision of Antwerp’s Summer Bummer festival taking place on a beach near a body of water. I had sunshine, seagull calls and good vibes in this fantasy. In reality, the venue, a rock club called Trix, is located on a busy road amongst high-rise apartment buildings just outside of downtown Antwerp. So, no seagulls, no beach and even the sun was being fickle. It troubled me, what could be the source for this misconception? The only part I had right was the ‘good vibes’. From the moment the first band started up in the darkened main hall on Friday afternoon to the closing tones of a bass-clarinet and electronics show on the intimate cafe stage late Saturday night, there was always something to hear, records to dig, people to talk shop with, and art to make — hardly leaving time to lament the waning days of the summer. Within the compact time-frame, starting late afternoon and ending around midnight on Friday and Saturday, festival organizers Koen Vandenhout and Christel Kumpen ran a tight program. Concerts were lined-up one after the other with a short break built-in to give the 200+ audience a chance to eat some dinner without developing FOMO. Plus, the sets ping-ponged from the main hall side to the cafe side, so there was always a chance to hit the bar if desired. Between the two halls, merch tables were arranged on all sides, making it dangerous to the wallet to traverse the venue. Parent organization of the festival Sound in Motion’s own Dropa-Disc label was present, as well as a record dealer with a selection of rare taste and local radio station Radio Centraal. If one purchased a t-shirt, or happened to have an extra one on hand, he or she (more likely than not: he) could head into the screen printing workshop and make their own with a festival design. Additionally, set in an adjacent room, musicians Cath Roberts and Tullis Rennie invited festival goers to record and manipulate sounds in a laboratory of their own design. When the weather was cooperative, one could visit the courtyard to procure some homemade food. Alexander von Schlippenbach and Paal Nilssen-Love The Sound In Motion website has the tagline, “Adventurous Music and Things”, and since we have got the things part out of the way, let us talk adventurous music . Not just a free-jazz festival, Summer Bummer’s scope this year included several avant-noise and electronics acts along with some of the most exciting musicians working (primarily) in Europe today. There was something for everyone, for example the ear-bleedingly loud Integral , a quartet comprised of Julien Desprez (guitar), Claire Gapenne (electronics and vocals), Christine Abelnour (sax) and Lukas Koenig (drums) that went from beguiling to battering, to the opening act, Kabas Sun Dogs, a Belgian band who had invited Canadian saxophonist Karen Ng and guitarist Jonathan Horne for a slowly unfolding exploration of both understatement and spirited groove. Rodrigo Amado, Joelle Leandre and Gerald Cleaver Highlights festooned the program, including a first time duo of drummer Paal Nilssen-Love and the legendary pianist Alexander von Schlippenbach as well as new trio formed by Rodrigo Amado with bassist Joelle Leandre and drummer Gerald Cleaver . In the duo’s extended set, Schlippenbach performed a chain of melodic ideas and Thelonius Monk song snippets that Nilssen-Love challenged with closely attuned force and precision. After a cautious opening, the trio of Amado, Leandre and Cleaver edged their way into the set, gathering momentum to the findcommon ground, letting Amado release his powerful tenor, Leandre impress with speed and expressiveness, and Cleaver move seamlessly between texture and forceful pulse. Daughter, Daughter The formidable quartet of Daughter, Daughter, comprised of Camila Nebbia and Amalie Dahl (saxophones), Elizabeth Coudoux (cello) and Sun Mi Hong (drums), performed a blend of composition and free-jazz improvisation showcasing both individual contributions as well as whole group interactions. The Berlin formation Das B , featuring Mazen Kerbaj (trumpet), Magda Mayas (piano), Tony Buck (drums) and Mike Majkowski (bass) was given the designation as a “super group“ in the program and their set did not refute this. Ostensibly deconstructing John Coltrane’s A Love Supreme , the quartet engaged in an exploratory and expansive sound collage complete with a trumpet played via surgical tubing and prepared piano that made the acoustic sound electric. Arguably one of the strongest shows of the festival. Das B Additionally, percussionist and singer Maria Portugal presented her EROSÃO Septet (Lotte Anker and Angelika Niescier on saxes , Matthias M üller and Moritz Wesp on trombones , Carl Ludwig H übsch on tuba and Reza Askari on bass ) , which performed a set of mid-tempo songs, both self-penned and from Brazilian composers, laced with some spicy improvisations. The next day, Portugal appeared in an exceptional duo with pianist Marta Warelis . As opposed to the septet, in which the music was a presented in more traditional structures, the songs themselves were de-composed and integrated organically with the ideas flowing from the pianist whose gentle and spacious playing grew progressively more ferocious. Marta Warelis and Maria Portugal Rounding out the program were two bass clarinet focused sets and several quite noisy ones. Representing the louder side, in addition to the aforementioned Integral, were New Best Friends (featuring Ng and Horne along with bassist Aaron Lumley and drummer Nasim L-P Navarro), the duo of Laurentiu Cotac and Diana Miron, and Mopcut with Desprez, Koenig and electronicist/vocalist Audrey Chen. Of these three, New Best Friends balanced their clamorous impulses best with a flowing set of improvisations. Bookending the festival were two bass clarinet sets. On the first day, John McCowen explored the extended tonalities of the acoustic contra-bass clarinet, exploiting the instrument’s multiphonic capabilities. Closing the festival, Hanna De Backer , in collaboration with the electronics of Yves De Mey , extended her instrument’s sonic possibilities to the outer realms. Overall, a musically adventurous and enjoyable festival, and although quite satisfied, I was still bothered by one thing: my imaginary festival on a beach. So, after some detective work, I believe I finally pinpointed the source of my whimsical misconception. In 2019, Rodrigo Amado's The Attic released the album Summer Bummer , recorded at the festival in 2018 and whose cover is an image of three cut-out figures sitting on a beach under a cloudless blue sky, looking out at the ocean. I didn’t know I was so impressionable! Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Ministry released its thirteenth studio album, “From Beer to Eternity”, on 6 September 2013 through 13th Planet Records. The album turns 13 this year. Al Jourgensen produced it with Sammy D’Ambruoso, recording between December 2012 and March 2013 at Jourgensen’s 13th Planet compound in El Paso, Texas. Dave Donnelly handled mastering. Jourgensen had said this would be Ministry’s final album, a plan later reversed with 2018’s “AmeriKKKant”. The sessions carried added weight: guitarist Mike Scaccia, whom Jourgensen described as the record’s driving force, died of a sudden heart attack three days after finishing his parts, while playing onstage with his other band, Rigor Mortis. Jourgensen and D’Ambruoso spent three months finishing the album afterward. Jourgensen recalled the tracking sessions themselves as smooth: “We have never, in the history of Ministry, ever had a tracking session like that before. Everything went so smoothly, it was surreal.” What is on Ministry’s ‘From Beer to Eternity’ The standard edition runs 11 tracks and 54:43: “Hail to His Majesty (Peasants)”, “Punch in the Face”, “PermaWar”, “Perfect Storm”, “Fairly Unbalanced”, “The Horror”, “Side F/X Include Mikey’s Middle Finger (TV4)”, “Lesson Unlearned”, “Thanx but No Thanx”, “Change of Luck” and “Enjoy the Quiet”. A Best Buy deluxe edition added “PermaWar Remix” and “Thanks for the Dub Remix”; the LP edition added a “Punch in the Face Remix”. “Thanx but No Thanx” sets William S. Burroughs’s poem “A Thanksgiving Prayer” to music, read by Sgt. Major, who had appeared on Ministry’s 2006 album “Rio Grande Blood”. Jourgensen sang and played guitar, keyboards and harmonica across the record. Scaccia and Sin Quirin played guitars, Tony Campos played bass on several tracks, and Aaron Rossi played drums. D’Ambruoso handled drum programming, synthesizer programming and co-production, and Aaron Havill contributed theremin, synthesizer and additional engineering. “PermaWar” served as the sole single, released through the iTunes Store on 9 August 2013. The cover art, by photographer Allan Amato, depicted seven models styled as sexualized, monster-like personifications of the seven deadly sins. It drew mockery from The A.V. Club’s Josh Modell, who compared it to Spinal Tap’s fictional “Smell the Glove” cover; Ministry responded with an alternate cover titled “Whole Lotta Glove” as a joke. “From Beer to Eternity” was also the first Ministry album since 2004’s “Houses of the Molé” without Tommy Victor on guitar or bass. The album reached number 140 on the Billboard 200 and number 7 on Billboard’s Hard Rock Albums chart. A remix companion, “From Beer to Eternamix”, followed on 22 November 2015. About Ministry Ministry formed in Chicago in 1981 around Al Jourgensen, mixing synth-pop on the 1983 debut “With Sympathy” before Jourgensen redirected the project toward the harder industrial sound that defined the band from “Twitch” (1986) onward. “The Land of Rape and Honey” (1988) and “The Mind Is a Terrible Thing to Taste” (1989) established the template of sampled vocals, distorted guitars and programmed rhythm that ran through the band’s most widely covered period, “Psalm 69: The Way to Succeed and the Way to Suck Eggs” (1992), which included the singles “N.W.O.” and “Jesus Built My Hotrod”. Jourgensen kept Ministry active through a long run of collaborators across the 1990s and 2000s, including “Filth Pig” (1996), “Dark Side of the Spoon” (1999), and a politically charged trilogy opened by “Houses of the Molé” (2004) and closed by “The Last Sucker” (2007), after which Jourgensen first announced the band’s retirement. He revived Ministry for “Relapse” (2012) and, after “From Beer to Eternity” in 2013, again for “AmeriKKKant” (2018), “Amerikkkant” follow-up “Moral Hygiene” (2021), and “HOPIUMFORTHEMASSES” (2021). Thirteen years on, Scaccia’s contributions to “From Beer to Eternity” remain the guitarist’s last studio recordings with the band he had rejoined multiple times since first playing on 1989’s “The Mind Is a Terrible Thing to Taste”.
items._cn_summary: Ministry的第十三张录音室专辑《From Beer to Eternity》是乐队一段沉重历史的见证。吉他手Mike Scaccia在完成录音后突发心脏病去世，Al Jourgensen与Sammy D'Ambruoso在余下三个月里完成了后期制作。音乐上延续了乐队标志性的工业金属冲击，融合鞭挞金属的暴力节奏与电子化编排，歌曲如“PermaWar”“Punch in the Face”充满政治讽刺与攻击性。特别之处在于“Thanx but No Thanx”将William S. Burroughs的诗《A Thanksgiving Prayer》配上音乐，由Sgt. Major朗读。专辑还因封面恶搞事件引发关注，并曾被视为Ministry的告别之作。整体上是一张情绪沉重、制作精良的工业金属作品，但并未对类型边界进行突破。

items.body: Tokyo darkwave and post-punk act Sex Virgin Killer followed its album “ANGEL” with a remix single, “Lissajous (Shinobu Narita Remix),” released digitally on streaming platforms and Bandcamp on August 28, 2026, through the band’s own lilii sound loom. A CD and a “KiTalbum” edition follow on October 2, 2026, with pre-orders open on Bandcamp since September 4. “Lissajous” is the closing track on “ANGEL,” the album Sex Virgin Killer released in International and Japanese versions in March 2026. The remix marks the second time Shinobu Narita has reworked the band’s material, after his 2023 remix of “The Lights Will Fall.” Narita fronted the electronics and guitar on the 1980s Japanese group Urban Dance, an offshoot of the minimal wave act 4-D, and later worked as a producer on Boris’s 2014 album “Noise.” Lissajous (Shinobu Narita Remix) by Sex Virgin Killer Shinobu Narita reworks ‘Lissajous’ for a limited CD and KiTalbum The CD edition, limited to 200 copies in a paper jacket, carries three tracks: “Lissajous (Shinobu Narita Remix),” “The Lights Will Fall (Shinobu Narita Remix)” and an instrumental version of the “Lissajous” remix. The KiTalbum edition adds the original International and Japanese versions of “Lissajous” from “ANGEL,” for five tracks total. Sex Virgin Killer recorded “Lissajous” at lilii sound loom and Studio Noah with Aisha on vocals, Lilii Mar on vocals, guitars, bass and synthesizers, and Hammer on drums, percussion and electronics. Narita handled the remix and mastering, with volume alignment by Soichiro Nakamura of Peace Music. Photo direction and styling for the release come from Atsuo of Boris, with photography by Yoshihiro Mori. A teaser video for the remix is posted on the band’s YouTube channel. About Sex Virgin Killer Sex Virgin Killer formed in Tokyo in 2006 around Lilii Mar, also known as masa, who came from the city’s hardcore punk scene. The band was active through 2018 playing a melodic metal sound tied to visual-kei, then went on hiatus before resuming activity in 2021. In 2023, Lilii Mar relaunched Sex Virgin Killer as a darkwave project alongside vocalist Aisha and drummer Hammer, moving the sound toward darkwave, post-punk, gothic rock and deathrock. That year also brought the single “The Lights Will Fall” and its first Shinobu Narita remix, followed by the second album “DEVIL” in November 2023, the EP “Heaven” in January 2024 and “Visual Shock Noise” in November 2024. In March 2026, the band released “ANGEL” in two editions: an International version on vinyl and digipak CD through Young & Cold Records, mixed and mastered by Daniel Hallhuber with art direction by Atsuo of Boris, and a Japanese version on cassette and CD through lilii sound loom, mixed by Yui Kimijima with cover art by Keigo Kurematsu. Sex Virgin Killer toured Europe in July 2026 behind the album. “Lissajous (Shinobu Narita Remix)” extends that album cycle with a new take on its closing song.
items._cn_summary: 东京暗潮乐队Sex Virgin Killer为专辑《ANGEL》的闭幕曲《Lissajous》推出Shinobu Narita混音版，以数字、CD及KiTalbum形式发行。混音版保留了原曲的暗潮与后朋克气质，并融入Narita曾参与Urban Dance和制作Boris专辑《Noise》的电子与噪音处理经验。CD限量200张，收录混音版、旧作《The Lights Will Fall》混音版及纯器乐版；KiTalbum版本另含国际版和日版原曲。作品录制由Aisha与Lilii Mar担纲人声与多乐器演奏，Hammer负责鼓与电子部分，混音与母带由Narita完成。整体来看，这首混音作品在原有哥特摇滚与死亡摇滚底色上，通过电子化重编拓展了声响维度，并延续乐队自2023年转向暗潮后的创作路径。

items.body: American ambient/electronic composer Steve Roach has released “The Current Above: Immersion Seven” on Projekt Records. The album came out on September 4, 2026, Bandcamp Friday, in a limited-edition CD (500 copies, 4-panel digipak), a limited-edition cassette (100 copies), and a name-your-price digital download. The Current Above: Immersion Seven by Steve Roach The album consists of a single 76-minute track, “The Current Above” (75:53). It continues the long-form Immersion series of ambient recordings that Roach began in the late 1990s, following on from Immersion Six, released in late 2025 as “The Surface Below” alongside a reissue of “Stillpoint”. Projekt describes the new record as a steady-state, low-volume listening environment built from slowly shifting textures and atmospheres, intended for settings such as sleeping, reading, and meditation. About Steve Roach Steve Roach is an American ambient/electronic composer who has worked in the genre since the early 1980s. He records from his longtime Timehouse studio in Baja Arizona. His catalog includes two Grammy nominations, for “Spiral Revelation” (2017) and “Molecules of Motion” (2018), both in the New Age Album category. Side-Line has tracked Roach’s recent output, including the 2025 announcement of “The Surface Below” and the “Stillpoint” reissue, and the 2026 announcement of the live 2CD “La Rosa – Live in Tucson, 2025”. “The Current Above: Immersion Seven” extends the Immersion series to a seventh volume, continuing an ambient practice Roach has maintained for more than four decades.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Steve Roach沉浸系列第七卷，核心为一首76分钟的长曲。作品延续了该系列长期以来的氛围音乐实践，以缓慢变化的音色纹理与低音量稳定状态构建聆听环境，适合睡眠、阅读或冥想等场景。Projekt Records发行了限量500张CD、100张磁带及自愿付费数字下载。作为一位自1980年代初持续创作的环境电子音乐家，Roach在这张作品中展现了他数十年如一日的沉浸式声响探索，没有强烈戏剧化推进，而是让声音在时间中自然延展，呈现出一种近乎静态的深度聆听体验。

items.body: In an instant, your anxiety turned into fear. Every sacrifice needs an audience. In older ceremonies, the victim did more than die: one body was converted into communal relief, the crowd watched the exchange, and authority called the loss necessary. Modern systems rarely build stone altars, but the underlying bargain survives. Work, debt, status, and belonging keep asking for portions of the self until surrender becomes ordinary enough to pass for participation. Las Vegas K-Goth trio Past Self brings that bargain into view in their new video for 제물 / Jemul. Released during the band’s ongoing European tour, the clip was shot and directed by Kameren Isaguirre from a screenplay by vocalist and guitarist Sung Joo Kim. Isaguirre also edited the video and produced it alongside Past Self. The song’s premise treats contemporary life as a form of spiritual extortion: a social order that takes money, time, dignity, and private feeling in exchange for continued membership. Echo-heavy guitar figures hang above a steady rhythm section while Sung’s Korean and English vocals follow anxiety into fear, hallucination, betrayal, and ruined love. The music bears traces of The Cure and Lebanon Hanover, along with the broader dramatic scale of The Horrors and the saturated guitar mass of My Bloody Valentine, yet Past Self keeps each part legible beneath the distortion. When we first covered the single, the band explained its central metaphor: “제물 / Jemul translates to ‘an offering,’” says the band. “It refers to a society that constantly demands a piece of one’s soul as payment for being allowed to stay alive. The song aims to draw metaphorical ties between this concept and human sacrifices that a cult might make to appease their deities.” Isaguirre brings that concept to life in the song’s enigmatic and arcane visual. Sung appears among dry reeds and bare trees, his face painted white, his lips black, and his eyes sealed beneath a broad red blindfold. Dark stains spread across his loose white blouse as he carries a cloth-bound sword through the brush, raises it toward the sky, and performs with a red guitar. The blindfold makes him both marked victim and sightless officiant: he cannot see the spectators, though the camera is always watching him. A vast red disc glows behind a black field of branches. A single rose lies in disturbed soil, and the sword is planted beside it, turning the landscape into altar and grave at once. Elsewhere, a second blindfolded figure appears collapsed on a concrete slab before slowly rising beneath the final blue light of dusk. The images never settle into a literal execution. Instead, they suggest preparation, selection, and aftermath, leaving sacrifice as a role that can pass from one body to another. Night changes the video’s visual grammar. A severe blue-white lamp blows out faces and fabric as the trio plays in tall grass. Movement smears across the frame, bodies divide into doubles, and horizontal scan lines make the footage resemble a damaged transmission. By the final wide shot, a lone figure sits beside a small table among the weeds, reduced nearly to evidence. The altar described in the lyrics has become an anonymous stretch of land under surveillance. The red blindfold is the video’s most effective device: it blocks the subject’s vision while leaving him completely available to ours. In a song about society exacting payment from the soul, visibility becomes another fee. The victim may be unable to identify the crowd, but the crowd has no trouble identifying the victim. Watch the video for 제물 / Jemul below: Written by Sung Joo Kim and mixed and mastered by Spektor, 제물 / Jemul is available to order through Past Self’s Bandcamp. 제물 / Jemul by past self Past Self are currently completing their debut European tour before returning to North America for dates in October and November. items._cn_summary: 拉斯维加斯三人乐队Past Self在这支单曲中将现代生活比作一场灵魂的持续献祭，隐喻社会以金钱、时间、尊严和私人情感换取成员的存续资格。音乐层面，回声吉他音色悬浮于稳定的节奏之上，韩英双语人声将焦虑推入恐惧、幻觉、背叛与爱之废墟的叙事弧线；编曲借鉴了The Cure与Lebanon Hanover的冷暗气质，同时吸收The Horrors的戏剧化张力与My Bloody Valentine的吉他音墙饱和度，但每一层元素都在失真下保持清晰可辨。音乐录影带由Kameren Isaguirre执导拍摄，视觉延续歌曲的核心隐喻：主唱面部涂白、唇部涂黑、眼部覆以红色宽幅盲带，行走于枯苇与光秃林木之间，手持布裹长剑与红色吉他，将整片荒原转化为祭坛与墓地的合一空间。夜场画面以蓝白灯光冲刷面部轮廓，水平扫描线与运动模糊制造仪式感与不安。整支作品以宗教献祭的古老框架映射当代生存的结构性代价，视觉与音乐共同构建出一个关于自愿牺牲与系统性索取的封闭剧场。

items.body: Strange to dream of you forever Even though I am wide awake The internet has abolished one of heartbreak’s few mercies: absence. Distance once allowed an attachment to lose oxygen, but the person we cannot stop thinking about now remains permanently available behind glass: photographs to revisit, timestamps to decode, and small signs of life that can be mistaken for an invitation to reminisce. Longing begins to resemble shift work, maintained around the clock by a thumb moving across a screen while the body waits somewhere else. That continuous state of checking and conjecture lies at the center of 24/7, the latest single and video from Pissoir des Dieux. The collaborative project brings together Larissa Iceglass of Lebanon Hanover, Vincenzo Wieczerzynski of Chaos International, and Owen Pratt of Uncanny Valley. Following their 2025 debut single, Hotel Grand Amour, the trio now announces their self-titled debut album, due September 28, 2026, through Fabrika Records. 24/7 begins with lightly strummed acoustic guitar and Iceglass’s breathy singing suspended in airy reverb. The arrangement is stripped down and emotionally exposed, carrying a bittersweet warmth without smoothing away its unease. Around the fifty-second mark, broad drums enter with a gentle crash as a thick, repeated bass figure gives the song a more regulated gait. Acoustic materials and machine-minded repetition begin working together, like an old mill keeping time at the edge of a forest. Near the two-and-a-half-minute mark, the bass drops into a deeper, slower, and more melodic sequence, turning the song toward something private and difficult to recover. It feels like watching an old home movie whose people can still move but can no longer answer. Bright guitar notes rise and fall through the closing passage, tracing small points of light like fireflies moving between the trees. Beneath that gentle surface, Iceglass describes attachment as a form of dependency. The absent person persists through photographs, clothing choices, questions about their safety, and even the condition of their keyboard; ordinary details accumulate until browsing becomes a self-administered dose. There is dry humour in the specificity, but it only makes the fixation feel more intimate. The phrase 24/7 becomes both a schedule and a diagnosis. Iceglass extends that idea into the video she directed and edited. Presented as grainy 4:3 camcorder footage, it carries date stamps for July 23 and July 24, 2025. Scenes from a birthday gathering at a country house—friends in the garden, rabbits in an enclosure, a dartboard, and an outdoor meal—alternate with close shots of Iceglass singing alone in a dim interior. At times her face is fully visible; elsewhere it appears as a pale fragment caught within a narrow strip of light. During the final passage, Iceglass leaves the house and enters the water beside a small dock, eventually lifting a glass above the surface. The footage possesses the factual appearance of a family tape, but its emotional status remains unresolved. It could be remembrance, fantasy, evidence, or the kind of saved material repeatedly replayed after direct contact has ended. The camera preserves a summer day with ruthless efficiency while the song considers what that preservation does to the person who cannot stop looking. Watch the video for 24/7 below: Pissoir des Dieux announce their eight-track self-titled debut album, arriving September 28, 2026 through Fabrika Records. Mixed by Owen Pratt and mastered by Schwebung Mastering, the record includes Hotel Grand Amour, 24/7, and six additional songs. Limited black, opaque, and pink vinyl editions are available, with each pressing limited to 500 copies. Listen to 24/7 below and pre-order Pissoir des Dieux here. items._cn_summary: Pissoir des Dieux是由Lebanon Hanover的Larissa Iceglass、Chaos International的Vincenzo Wieczerzynski和Uncanny Valley的Owen Pratt组成的合作项目。单曲24/7以轻拨的原声吉他开场，Iceglass气声般的演唱悬浮在空灵的混响中，编曲克制而情感外露。随后鼓组与反复的低音线条引入，带来类似古老磨坊的机械节奏感。歌词将依恋描述为一种依赖——照片、衣物选择、安全状况的询问，浏览行为如同自我给药，24/7既是时间表也是诊断。Iceglass自导自演的MV采用颗粒感4:3录像带画幅，记录生日聚会与独自歌唱的场景交替，最终以她走入水中举起玻璃杯的画面收尾。整首作品以原声质感与机械重复的对比为核心，探讨数字时代缺席感的瓦解，与暗潮传统中对情感疏离的持续关注一脉相承。

items.body: Bands: Cocanha, Los Sara Fontán, Tarta Relena | Album: 4132314 | Genre: Experimental folk | Bandcamp This collaboration of three duos is a mixture of original compositions and reinterpretations of folk songs. Cocanha specializes in Occitan polyphony, Los Sara Fontán in Catalan folk, and Tarta Relena in electronic-tinged post-rock; and all three bands’ styles are on proud display here. The vocals are rich, multi-layered, and carefully arranged; and the backing is brimming with odd metrical flourishes. This record feels like it has one foot in the twenty-first century and another in the nineteenth, and it’s a fantastic mash-up. Score: 86/100 Band: Furii | Album: Pyromancy | Genre: Progressive pop | Bandcamp Furii (pronounced “fury”) is a Cardiacs-adjacent project, a fact which is unmistakable from this album’s opening moments. Sole bandmember Adrien Rodes is the longtime keyboardist of Spratleys (another Tim Smith project) and an occasional member of Cardiacs’ live band. Joanne Spratley, another member of Spratleys, provides vocals on Pyromancy, and her vocals lend an eerie, airy atmosphere. The textures on this record are psychedelic and dreamy, with tinkling piano and swirling synths. Despite the songs being rather to-the-point, the soundscapes presented are dense and complex, with lots of innovative sonic choices. I found LSD to be an exhausting listen (and not in a fun way), but this is a much more enjoyable spiritual successor to Cardiacs. Score: 80/100 Band: Godsticks | Album: VOiD | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp Godsticks is a Welsh four-piece that plays a relatively heavy, alt-adjacent variety of progressive rock. This record is stuffed to the brim with flashy riffs, a rotating assortment of time signatures, and powerful vocals. None of the songs here are particularly long, but that focus pays off. Each piece features a powerful distillation of semi-metallic riffs and clever structuring. Quieter moments often feature some electronic embellishments, and I appreciate that tonal contrast. By the end of the record, things do start to sound a bit samey, but it’s still a solid release, overall. Score: 73/100 Band: Kaatayra | Album: Caminhos de Água | Genre: Post-metal, Progressive folk | Bandcamp This is a tough record to categorize with traditional genre labels. The band bills itself as acoustic black metal, and that really is the best summary, as odd as that sounds. Significant Brazilian folk influence is present here, as well. A friend showed me their 2021 album, Inpariquipê, and I thought it was interesting. My first impression was that it sounded like Incantations-era Mike Oldfield doing black metal, and I’ll reiterate that general impression here. Textures are lush, with various wind instruments and wooden idiophones lending sonic depth. This is an example of a record that, for me, at least, has benefitted from multiple listens. When I first heard it, I thought it was fine but I might need a little time to digest it. Each time I’ve come back to it, I’ve found something new to like or noticed some new intricacy I’d previously missed.  The album’s title (Portuguese for “Waterways”) is fitting, with the music here invoking rivers perfectly. There are moments of gentle relaxation as it flows and burbles. In contrast, there are moments where high-tempo rapids and waterfalls of anxiety and tension crash down upon the listener. Score: 87/100 Band: Slift | Album: Fantasia | Genre: Heavy psych, Space rock | Bandcamp Slift’s fourth LP sees them scale things back. My main complaint about Ilion was its crushing, unnecessary length. Fantasia features plenty of artsy, kraut-inspired riffage and soaring, interstellar textures alongside the band’s garage rock roots. But it’s presented at a much more manageable length. The emotion comes through clear as day in these songs, complementing the raw power of the compositions. Score: 81/100 Band: Spell | Album: Wretched Heart | Genre: Heavy metal, Progressive rock | Bandcamp The latest release from this Canadian traditional heavy metal quartet might be my favorite from them yet. In some ways, this record reminds me of Voivod’s Angel Rat, in that metal is often toned down in favor of psychedelia, prog-rock, and post-punk. The synth tones on this record also lend it a spooky, gothic edge, which couples well with the band’s smart and complex melodic passages. There are dazzling solos aplenty, and the songs’ constant morphing and churning keep the listener engaged. Score: 84/100
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了四张风格各异的独立专辑评论，重点突出实验性与跨文化融合。法国-加泰罗尼亚地区三位女性二人组合作的《4132314》将奥克语、卡泰隆语复调与电子元素揉合，节奏变化丰富，声部编排精致，呈现出十九世纪民间音乐与当代声响的交汇。Furii的《Pyromancy》延续了Cardiacs式的疯克前卫血脉，键盘铺底营造迷幻梦境感，是该传统中较为易入口的精神续作。Godsticks的《VOiD》走重型前卫摇滚路线，节奏型多变但后期略显雷同。Kaatayra的《Caminhos de Água》最具个性，将巴西民间乐器与原声黑金属嫁接，木质打击与管乐器为极端人声增添丰富层次，需要多次聆听方能完全展开。整体而言，这些作品均来自独立厂牌与Bandcamp生态，强调个人化创作视角与跨界实验，与小众实验音乐审美高度契合。

items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.
items.label: Sunnyside SCS 1813
items._genre: avant-garde jazz / vocal improvisation / experimental piano
items._cn_summary: Ran Blake与Dominique Eade合作的专辑展现出极具个人色彩的钢琴-人声二重奏美学。Blake的曲目编排以罕见的并置著称，将Max Roach、Mingus等爵士经典与流行金曲、影视配乐乃至民谣并置，揭示作品间潜藏的结构与情感脉络，而非简单翻奏。Eade的声乐处理字斟句酌、情感外放，与Blake含蓄内敛的钢琴形成张力。她既非Billie Holiday式的深沉，也不过度克制，而是在Mingus的《Portrait》等暗色调曲目中仍透出鲜明的歌唱愉悦感。该专辑延续了Blake自与Jeanne Lee合作以来的实验性人声探索传统，同时以新材料组合拓展了学院派爵士人声二重奏的边界。

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑聚焦乌克兰东部被俄罗斯掳走的约两万儿童这一战争罪行主题，由乌克兰裔加拿大歌手Marichka联合两国音乐人共同创作。音乐以传统弓弦乐器为主，辅以班杜拉琴与钢琴，并融入乌克兰传统仪式歌曲元素。被摧毁的港口城市马里乌波尔出身的Lisa以双陶笛独奏参与录音，她本人年仅十六岁，曾是被掳走的儿童之一。歌曲以传统曲调与原创作品交织，歌词译文讲述母亲送别女儿远赴异乡、女儿化作飞鸟归来的悲剧故事。编曲在温柔的人声与粗粝的节奏间形成对比，呼应被掳儿童的哀痛与愤怒。专辑将乌克兰民间音乐传统与当代主题紧密结合，是一份具有文化深度的音乐回应。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是挪威Camilla Hole Trio在延续前作科幻合成器与传统素材结合的探索后，转向更'接地气'的创作。三位乐手以Soprano Sax、Double Bass与鼓为核心编制，引入模块合成器与颤音琴丰富音色层次。作品以西挪威传统Springleik舞曲旋律为起点，但演奏中角色不断流动，bass手Kalman与鼓手Nesheim的节奏与色彩支撑与Hole的旋律交织，随即兴展开而模糊了主从关系。整体呈现北欧爵士即兴美学与世界音乐素材的有机融合，配器克制而富有空间感，适合偏好实验爵士与跨界融合的听众深入聆听。

items.body:
A debut, digital-only EP from a Danish trio, led by one of the Nordic folk scene�s outstanding and experienced vocalists, Mia Guldhammer. Five tracks, with the musicians bringing their own perspectives to mostly traditional music. There�s a lovely ancient, creaky mood throughout.
The opener, �Svennedal,� with its rough, cantering rhythm, offers a perfect shop window for Guldhammer�s impressive, persuasive voice, while jaw harp and bagpipes bring an insistent propulsion to �Nordg�rd,� the only original here, by band member Morten Musicus.
Cimbalom adds a delicate backdrop to the traditional �Agnete Of Bjergmanden,� with Guldhammer�s soft jaw harp offering extra textures to the other instruments, as it brings a springy opening to the final cut, �Orms�,� mingling with flute and strings to create something quite thrilling and off kilter on this instrumental.
Five tracks, and an introduction to a band that already seems very mature and accomplished. A strong beginning � what will GuldGanger do with an entire album?

items._cn_summary: 这张丹麦三人组的数字迷你专辑包含五首作品，乐手以个人视角重新演绎传统北欧素材，整体弥漫古旧而粗粝的氛围。开场曲以粗糙、起伏的节奏与主唱富有说服力的嗓音构成醒目入口；口弦与风笛为唯一原创曲提供持续的推进感；钦巴龙为传统叙事曲铺陈精致底色；末段器乐曲中，口弦与长笛、弦乐交织出失衡却灵动的声响。作为首张短作，乐队已展现出成熟的默契与鲜明的声音个性。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.
